Discounting and Promotions

A discount is a purchase: you buy a named behaviour, at a price, from a named buyer. Two firms in Dibrugarh find neither can say what they bought.

1 Two decisions, five days apart

On 22 September 2026 Tridib Bordoloi, chief revenue officer of Orunodoi Sensor Networks, was looking at a chart he had asked for twice and wished he had not. Orunodoi, founded in Dibrugarh in 2021, made the Xitol node — a gateway and eight validated temperature sensors — and sold it with a monitoring subscription to pharmaceutical distributors and cold stores across the Northeast. The node listed at ₹1.20 lakh and the subscription at ₹4,000 per node per month; list prices had not moved in three years.

Two things bothered him. Fifteen points of list had gone in six quarters with no list-price decision taken; and Q2 FY27, which ran no scheme at all, recorded the series' lowest pocket price, 71.0 per cent. The discount had become the price. Buyers, Gunin Saikia reported from Tinsukia, no longer asked whether there was a scheme, only what this quarter's was.

Five days later, Gargi Hazarika, vice-president of product and pricing at Ekatra Telemetry Cloud, had a narrower problem of the same shape. Ekatra sold no hardware, only a compliance platform aligned to Schedule M of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and to WHO good distribution practice, at ₹9.60 lakh per warehouse per year, to 31 customers across 84 facilities. Nothing it discounted was ever published. On 25 September the procurement head of Enajori Coldstores, a cold-store operator with 26 facilities, asked for 45 per cent off list and a three-year price hold; bids were due 9 October. Tapan Deka, who ran the deal desk from Jorhat, had one sentence for it: whatever we sign becomes the number every renewal starts from for three years.

2 What a discount is, and the quarrel about what it costs

A discount is a reduction from list granted to a particular buyer, for a particular reason, for a particular period; a promotion is the same instrument made public and time-boxed, its trigger a date rather than a negotiation. A reduction that is not particular — everyone, indefinitely, for no stated reason — is a price cut nobody minuted.

Two traditions talk past each other. The first is price discrimination: charging differently-willing buyers different prices raises output and profit, if the seller can tell them apart and stop arbitrage. Its practical branch runs through Michael Marn and Robert Rosiello's 1992 account of the price waterfall — the cascade of discounts, rebates and off-invoice concessions separating list from the pocket price realised — and Thomas Nagle and Reed Holden's rule that a price change be judged against the volume needed to break even.

The second tradition is behavioural. Russell Winer established that buyers judge a price against an expectation formed by what they last attended to; Robert Blattberg and Scott Neslin found most of a promotional bump to be switching and acceleration rather than category expansion; Carl Mela, Sunil Gupta and Donald Lehmann showed sustained promotion makes buyers more price-sensitive. Here a discount's cost is what buyers expect next quarter.

3 Mechanics: the waterfall, the break-even, the counterfactual

Expert practice has three movements. The first builds the waterfall honestly, counting concessions nobody calls discounts. On Orunodoi's average Q2 FY27 node the invoice showed a ten per cent volume slab; the rest was invisible to the discount report.

The second restates the waterfall as contribution, because a discount is spent out of margin, not revenue: Orunodoi's hardware carries a real cost of goods, the subscription almost none.

At Q1 FY26 economics the ₹7,200 credit is 6.98 per cent of a ₹1,03,200 pocket price against a margin of 28.19 per cent, so volume must rise by 6.98 divided by 21.21, or 32.9 per cent. Nobody had named a number the scheme had to beat.

The third movement is the counterfactual, where most organisations stop. A bump is not an effect; the effect is the difference from what would have happened, and the instrument is a holdout read a period later, because acceleration repays itself out of the next quarter.

4 When the idea applies, stated as tests

The claim is conditional, and the conditions are testable.

Where the idea actively misleads is worth saying plainly. When the loss is not about price, a discount buys nothing and delays the diagnosis: Orunodoi lost four FY26 tenders to Oitijya Instruments over calibration certificates it could not supply. And when switching costs are high and rising — a validated Ekatra installation is re-qualified at the customer's cost — the conclusion inverts. Renewal is the moment to hold price, and the moment most firms discount hardest.

5 Hard edges: bundles, channels, regulation, inference

Bundles are the first hard edge. Orunodoi's deal is one hardware sale plus an annuity, and which component absorbs the discount is a permanent decision disguised as a tactical one. Three free months and ₹12,000 off hardware cost the same: ₹12,000 of revenue and, because the node is monitored throughout, ₹12,000 of contribution. Only one of them resets the price the customer sees again every year. Under Ind AS 115 a bundle discount is allocated across performance obligations by standalone selling price, so “free” months still recognise subscription revenue and reduce hardware revenue.

Channels are the second. Orunodoi reaches smaller cold stores in Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh through two system integrators, where a rupee given to the end customer and a rupee of integrator margin are the same rupee: deepen the scheme and the integrator's reason to prefer you weakens, which is how a firm cuts street price and loses share at once. Regulation is the third: public cold-chain buying routes through lowest-bidder tender, and a price quoted there becomes a durable public reference.

The fourth edge belongs to the AI layer. Ekatra's excursion-prediction model runs inference over every sensor stream, costed at ₹390 per sensor per year including ingest. A standard 80-sensor facility costs ₹0.31 lakh in inference within a total cost to serve of ₹1.68 lakh. A 600-sensor mega-warehouse costs ₹2.34 lakh, and with ₹1.37 lakh of fixed service cost its total is ₹3.71 lakh — so at the ₹4.32 lakh price of the deepest band it contributes ₹0.61 lakh, a margin of about 14 per cent against the 75.5 per cent on the average facility. Flat per-facility pricing, a deep discount and variable inference cost together make cash-negative customers, and none looks dangerous alone. At the seam this is invisible: the deal desk approves against list, and the model bill lands in engineering.

6 Eight things an expert notices

The denominator is contribution, not price

A deal desk authorising “up to 25 per cent” without knowing contribution margin governs nothing. Twenty-five per cent off a subscription at 77.5 per cent margin costs a third of contribution; off Orunodoi's hardware, at 28.19 per cent of pocket price, nearly all of it. The tell: an approval matrix with no margin column.

The cost of a promotion lands in the period after it

Acceleration is repaid. The diagnostic is not the promotion quarter but the accuracy of the next: a plan reliable in scheme quarters and optimistic afterwards describes pull-forward. Orunodoi's Q2 FY27 shortfall was read as a soft market for three weeks before April was blamed.

An unpublished discount is more dangerous than a published one

The obvious reading is that secrecy protects price. It does the opposite: a published scheme has an owner, an expiry and a ledger; a private concession none. The tell is a quarter with no scheme in which pocket price falls anyway — Orunodoi's Q2 FY27, migration out of the ledger into free sensors and documentation.

A fence must be observable and costly to cross

“New customers only” holds until a customer registers a new entity; “small facilities only” holds until the customer reports its own sensor count. Fences resting on self-description are decoration; those that hold attach to what the seller verifies: a commitment term, volume shipped, a site installed.

Volume commitments are the only self-funding fence, if breakage is enforced

A discount bought with a commitment converts a giveaway into an exchange, but only if under-delivery has a consequence — and the minimum is rarely audited, because whoever would audit it signed the deal. The tell: a contract file full of tiered pricing and a receivables file with no true-up invoices.

The pocket-price band, not the average, is the diagnostic

An average discount of 28.7 per cent describes nothing. Ekatra's 84 facilities run from ₹9.12 lakh to ₹4.32 lakh for the same product, a spread of 2.11 times, and that distribution determines what a new deal costs. Read the tail: 39 of the 84 facilities, or 46.4 per cent, sit below 70 per cent of list, so the credible floor is far beneath the average.

A discount given to win is conceded again at renewal, unless something changed

Firms tell themselves the first year is an investment recovered later. The evidence would be renewal uplift measured separately for discounted and undiscounted cohorts, and most have never computed it. Absent an escalator, a commitment or a product change the buyer values, repricing upward is unlikely.

“Time-limited” is a claim about the organisation, not the offer

Every scheme has an end date; the question is whether the firm has enforced one. Ask who owns the expiry, by name. If nobody answers in ten seconds, the offer is permanent and the list price fiction. Orunodoi had run its schemes three years with no decision to renew on record.

7 How it changes by product type and stage

In consumer markets the reference price resets quickly and festival promotion is close to a scheduling instrument; the hazard is a segment that buys only on offer. In B2B mid-market — Orunodoi's world — the price is remembered and travels, because buyers compare invoices. In enterprise the constraint inverts: prices are private, so the reference-price mechanism is weak, but the most-favoured-nation ratchet is strong and the binding cost is what a new floor does to renewals. Neither firm is two-sided, and the marketplace point — that a take-rate concession to one side is funded by the other — does not transfer. For hardware the break-even arithmetic bites harder; for AI-native products a variable cost floor makes safe discount depth customer-specific.

Stage matters too. At seed stage a heavy discount for a reference customer can be rational: credibility bought may exceed margin surrendered, and there is no installed base to contaminate. At the stage both firms occupy, every discount is a precedent. At scale, discounting becomes an architecture — a published ladder, an approval matrix keyed to contribution, a quarterly pocket-price review whose absence is itself the diagnosis.

One: the Bihu holdout, and three verdicts on one scheme

Three: the withdrawal that failed, and what recovery required

The instructive failure is Orunodoi's own. In July 2025 leadership suspended all schemes and told the field to hold list. The opening chart records the result: pocket price fell from 86.0 to 84.0 to 82.0 per cent of list while quarterly volume fell from 296 nodes to 268 and then 241, a decline of 18.6 per cent. Discipline had been announced, not built. With no fence and quota unchanged, representatives replaced the scheme with concessions needing no approval, and by January the year-end scheme was back, the wrong lesson learned.

Recovery required architecture, not instruction. The volume slab was published, so discount was earned by order size; the scheme credit was restricted to greenfield facilities, expiring 31 December 2026; the three free months became purchasable only against a 24-month commitment; and any concession beyond 15 per cent of list required Zinia Kakoti's approval, computed on contribution. A pocket price of 78 per cent of list then lifts hardware contribution from ₹11,669 to ₹19,800 a node — ₹8,131 more, or 69.7 per cent — worth ₹1.32 crore across an FY28 plan of 1,620 nodes.

9 Failure modes and their early warnings

Exhibit 8 · Three failure modes

Some are cheap to catch and some are not. Calendar reflex and off-ledger concession both surface in a monthly pocket-price series, which costs an analyst a day a month and which neither firm produced before September 2026. The ratchet is different: its sign is a single deal, its consequences arrive one to three years later, and by then the evidence that would have justified holding price cannot be created.

10 Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is about horizon. The lifetime-value position holds that a discount acquiring an annuity is an acquisition cost like any other, and judging it on first-year contribution a category error; Orunodoi's numbers support it, the scheme being worth ₹10.11 lakh over a lifetime and minus ₹13.86 lakh in year one. It rests on discounted cohorts retaining and on renewal pricing recovering, and is wrong if either fails. Most firms asserting it have measured neither.

The second is about what a discount costs. The reference-price camp argues the giveaway is trivial beside the shift in expectation, pointing at ₹1.47 crore against ₹19.97 lakh. The counter is not that the mechanism is false but that its scope is narrower than claimed: established on frequently-purchased consumer goods, it is weak where the buyer is a procurement function pricing off comparables. Ekatra is a genuine test case, unresolved.

The third is whether measurement is possible at all. The holdout school insists no promotion run without one, which is right and frequently impossible: Ekatra has 31 customers and a single tender. The everyday-low-price school treats that as an argument against the instrument: an unmeasurable lever with a known organisational cost is a bad lever. The rebuttal is the third example above. What would settle it is evidence nobody has — a firm that removed promotion, held a fence three years and published its pocket-price series.

11 What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this argues about the discount percentage. Someone who has internalised it changes the question. They ask what behaviour is being purchased before what it costs, and can name it in a sentence. They quote pocket price, having counted the concessions nobody calls discounts, and never approve a discount without naming the fence. And they hold two numbers at once: what this deal costs, and what it costs the renewal book.

12 What each of them decided

Tridib did not cancel the scheme. He converted it into the architecture above and added one standing instrument: Jorhat–Golaghat becomes a permanent holdout, so the counterfactual is always available. He gave the board a target of 78 per cent of list by Q4 FY27, reported monthly, tolerating lower volume meanwhile. The fifteen-point slide had never been decided by anyone; the first job was not to price better but to make pricing a decision again.

Gargi bid 37.5 per cent off, ₹6.00 lakh per facility, against a request for 45. She attached three things the deeper bid could not carry: a three-year price hold escalating with inflation, capped at five per cent; a volume trigger stepping price to ₹5.28 lakh if Enajori reaches 40 facilities, which at a cost to serve of ₹2.28 lakh across 40 sites is worth ₹120.00 lakh of contribution against ₹88.40 lakh at 26; and a written statement that the price is consideration for the 26-facility commitment, so the fence exists on paper. She would rather lose this bid, she told Tapan, than win the next three renegotiations.

For discussion. First: the scheme is worth minus ₹13.86 lakh in year one and plus ₹10.11 lakh over a lifetime — which belongs on the slide, and what must you believe to defend the other? Second: Gargi's fence is a contract clause, Tridib's an order-size slab; which survives a sales force? Third: if Ekatra cannot build a holdout, what is the next-best evidence that a discount bought something, and is it good enough to bet ₹137.28 lakh on?

13 Going deeper

Value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing sets the list price this topic discounts from. Deal desk, discounting and exceptions builds the machinery Tridib invented. Trade promotions and gross-to-net is the accounting discipline for off-invoice credits, the part of the waterfall that escapes the discount report. Discount architecture is the design problem: how many rungs, keyed to what, exchanged for what. When to charge decides whether a concession is best given as price, payment terms or term length. Willingness-to-pay research supplies the segment estimates a fence must separate. The value metric fixes what you discount per unit of; Ekatra's inference problem is a value-metric problem in a discount costume. Packaging: good / better / best is the alternative: give less rather than charge less. Freemium vs free trial is the same trade at zero, and What pricing signals closes the loop, since buyers read a discount as a claim about worth.

Kasauti Safety Exchange: The Last Fortnight of the Quarter

A decision case on discounting and promotions

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday 1 October 2026, Urmi Chokshi sat in the glass-walled meeting room on the second floor of the Kasauti Safety Exchange office in Vadodara, with the second-quarter close open on her laptop. The quarter had ended the previous night with the usual rush of orders, almost every one carrying a discount negotiated by phone.

Chokshi, the head of commercial, had until Thursday 15 October to give the founder a pricing plan for the October to December quarter. That quarter included Diwali in early November. The sales team wanted a festival campaign. She wondered whether the company already ran one every quarter, unannounced.

2. Company background

Kasauti Safety Exchange sells industrial safety equipment online to factories, contractors and facility managers: helmets, full-body harnesses, cut-resistant gloves and fire extinguishers. Dhaval Mankad, a former plant-safety officer at a Vadodara petrochemical unit, founded it in 2019. Every item has a published list price, exclusive of GST, and products meet Bureau of Indian Standards specifications. Forty-six people work for it.

Customers sit in the belt from Vadodara through Bharuch and Dahej, and increasingly in Tamil Nadu. Rivals are larger. Moglix and IndiaMART list thousands of suppliers and give buyers instant comparison, and Amazon Business has added a safety category. Kasauti competes on delivery speed, certified stock and service, not on being cheapest.

3. The situation

List price, in practice, had become a starting offer. Over the first half of the financial year, April to September 2026, sales representatives discounted almost every deal, and each discount was approved by the sales head alone. Lata Sheth, the finance controller, pulled the data together. Exhibit 1 sets it out by product category.

Two facts stood out. First, on list prices the half-year would have produced gross margin of ₹400.5 lakh, 47.1 per cent of ₹850.0 lakh. The company kept ₹219.5 lakh, so discounting consumed ₹181.0 lakh. Each percentage point of discount cost about ₹8.5 lakh. Second, helmets and gloves, the items customers compare online, carried the deepest discounts, 25 and 30 per cent. A helmet listed at ₹400 and costing ₹220 earned ₹180 at list and only ₹80 at the realised average of ₹300, so volume would have had to rise from 40,000 to 90,000 units, or 125 per cent, to recover the margin. It had not.

The discounts also stacked. A harness sold to a Bharuch chemical plant in September began at ₹2,500. The representative gave 20 per cent for the relationship, the sales head added 10 per cent for order size, and the customer asked for and received 5 per cent more for signing before quarter-end. Exhibit 2 follows the price down.

The deal earned ₹460 a harness, 37 per cent of what list would have earned. The customer, Uday Amin, procurement head at a chemical plant near Dahej, told her he held orders until the last fortnight of a quarter because Kasauti always gave more then. Exhibit 3 tests whether he was typical.

Share of deals landing in the final fortnight had risen from 40 to 50 per cent in one quarter, and the average discount in that window was 26.4 per cent against 14.5 per cent for the rest of the time. Customers had been trained. Yatin Thakkar, the sales head, read the same numbers as proof that quarter-end urgency worked.

4. The people

Urmi Chokshi, head of commercial, Vadodara, owns pricing and reports to the founder. She wants a policy she can explain. Yatin Thakkar, sales head, works from the Coimbatore office that opened last year to serve Tamil Nadu. He carries a quarterly target. He wants a campaign and continued discretion. Lata Sheth, finance controller, Vadodara, built the exhibits and wants discounts that can be traced to a rule. Dhaval Mankad, founder and chief executive, wants an annual revenue run-rate of ₹15 crore by March and worries about losing accounts to Moglix. Uday Amin, the customer, is not in the boardroom, but his behaviour is the evidence.

5. The options

Option A: A Diwali festival campaign. Yatin Thakkar proposes an extra 10 per cent off realised prices across the catalogue for orders placed between 15 October and 15 November,. The upside is momentum. The cost is arithmetic. On the half-year's volumes, 10 per cent off the realised ₹669.0 lakh removes ₹66.9 lakh, leaving revenue of ₹602.1 lakh and gross margin of ₹152.6 lakh against ₹219.5 lakh, or 25.3 per cent of revenue. Volume would need to rise 43.8 per cent for margin rupees to break even.

Option B: A published volume schedule, with no quarter-end discount. Kasauti would replace negotiation with a schedule visible on the site. Orders below ₹1 lakh at list value carry no discount, orders of ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh carry 8 per cent, and orders above ₹5 lakh carry 12 per cent. A buyer who signs an annual rate contract with quarterly drawdowns earns a further 5 per cent, which stacks to 16.4 per cent at most (1 minus 0.88 x 0.95). Sheth's model assumes the blended discount settles at 15 per cent. On the half-year's volumes that gives revenue of ₹722.5 lakh, gross margin of ₹273.0 lakh, or 37.8 per cent, ₹53.5 lakh more if volumes hold. Volume could fall 19.6 per cent before margin rupees drop below today's ₹219.5 lakh. The risk is that price-sensitive accounts in helmets and gloves will leave for online marketplaces.

Option C: A deal desk with floors and approval tiers. Representatives may discount to 10 per cent, the sales head to 20 per cent, and anything above goes to Chokshi. A floor of 25 per cent gross margin on realised price is set: about ₹293 for a helmet, ₹1,667 for a harness, ₹90 for gloves and ₹2,400 for an extinguisher. The upside is control with little disruption. The cost is that it fixes only the deepest deals. Helmets already average ₹300, barely ₹7 above their floor, and quarter-end timing is untouched. Customers such as Amin still learn to wait.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what does discounting cost Kasauti, and where is it least defensible?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 show how the price falls and when. What has Kasauti taught its customers?
  3. Compare the three options on margin, and on the customer behaviour each creates.
  4. Which option would you take to the founder on 15 October, and what would change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is a simple test: a discount creates value only when it buys something the company would not otherwise get, such as volume, commitment, a new segment or the clearing of surplus stock. A discount any customer can obtain by waiting buys nothing; it teaches waiting. Exhibit 3 is the diagnostic: when half of all deals land in the last fifteen days at nearly twice the discount, the calendar, not the product, is setting the price.

A well-reasoned answer starts from the unit economics in Exhibit 1, notes the stacking in Exhibit 2, and judges each option by the behaviour it rewards. Option A is weakest: it adds a publicised discount for customers already conditioned to wait, and needs a 43.8 per cent volume increase to break even. Option C treats the symptom.

Sauda Materials Exchange: What Did We Discount?

An ambiguous case on discounting and promotions

1. Sunday night, Raipur

On Sunday 11 October 2026, a little after ten at night, Jagriti Dewangan sat at her dining table in Raipur with two printed schedules beside her and a third open on the laptop. All three described the same quarter of trading at Sauda Materials Exchange, 1 July to 30 September 2026, all produced by people she trusted. They said the company had discounted 11.7 per cent, 12.8 per cent and 16.2 per cent.

The pricing committee met at nine. As chief commercial officer, Jagriti owned the rate plate, the discount grid, the channel schemes and the annual rebate ladder, and was expected to bring one number and a policy. What she had was a suspicion that the number did not exist: that "we discounted 11.7 per cent" was not a fact about a transaction but a sentence with four defensible completions.

At 9.40 Hania Zielinska, the contract data scientist who rebuilt the margin dashboard from Kraków, sent one line: "Tell me which boundary you want the price measured at. I can build any of them. I cannot build all of them into one figure." Jagriti was looking at a September order for 480 tonnes of TMT bar, and at four colleagues holding four prices for it.

2. How Sauda got here

Sauda Materials Exchange was founded in Raipur in 2019 to do one unglamorous thing well: let a builder, contractor or dealer order TMT bar, structural steel, cement and admixtures on a screen, at a stated price, with delivery to site and credit. Chhattisgarh suited it: short-haul supply from the state's mills, and dealers who negotiated by telephone.

By September 2026 it employed 318 people and traded in two quite different ways. Under Loha Direct it bought on its own balance sheet and invoiced the buyer: revenue, cost of goods, freight and credit risk all Sauda's. Under the Maang Board it brokered, a mill or large dealer supplying the buyer directly while Sauda took a commission scheduled at 1.6 per cent of board value. Buyers on 30-, 60- or 90-day terms used Seemant Credit, funded from a ₹120 crore consortium line, ₹96 crore drawn at quarter-end.

Two earlier decisions constrain what is available to her now. In January 2024, to make the marketplace feel trustworthy rather than bazaar-like, Sauda published a single rate plate for the whole country, promised to revise it only at the start of a financial year, and honoured any quoted plate price for seven days. In April 2024, to stop the sales team fighting over which book an order landed in, the incentive was fixed at ₹85 a tonne of steel and ₹4 a cement bag, identical on own-book and brokered volume.

3. The industry

Building materials in India is a trade of published prices that nobody pays. The integrated producers — SAIL's Bhilai Steel Plant an hour away, Jindal Steel at Raigarh, JSW and Tata Steel nationally — issue trade price circulars that move with ore, coking coal and import parity, and moved twice in the quarter; cement's majors publish bag prices that vary by district. Standards are not negotiable: TMT bar is bought to IS 1786 as Fe 500D, cement to IS 269. Price is almost the only axis left, and the competition does not agree on a model: Infra.Market and OfBusiness built own-book businesses, Moglix and IndiaMART sit closer to pure marketplaces, JSW One Platform brings a producer's distribution online.

Regulation shapes the mechanics. GST e-invoicing covers every Sauda invoice, TMT bar attracts GST at 18 per cent and cement at 28 per cent, and a post-supply discount reduces taxable value only where it was agreed at or before supply and linked to invoices. The Reserve Bank's attention to trade credit has made the lenders more interested in receivable days than growth. Nor is the exposure only domestic: Bin Haider Contracting LLC of Sharjah, building in Doha, wanted 5,400 tonnes through Paradip.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 is the quarter as the management accounts present it, and the source of the board pack's headline: ₹36.26 crore of discount against ₹309.90 crore of plate value, 11.70 per cent.

On 25 September Hania's dashboard broke TMT bar into fortnights, and Exhibit 2 dismantled the plate. The plate had not moved since April; the mills revised twice, up in August and part-way back in September, and Sauda's cost followed. Measured off plate, the discount wandered between 9.91 and 13.22 per cent while pricing behaviour barely changed; measured off the mill's trade price landed at Raipur, the same tonnes were discounted between 0.59 and 4.77 per cent.

August cost real money: 3,100 tonnes shipped on quotes issued before Sauda's cost rose ₹2,300 a tonne, ₹71.30 lakh surrendered and none of it recorded as discount, because the plate had not changed.

Then came the order. On 18 September Sauda shipped 480 tonnes of Fe 500D to account BSP-114, a Bilaspur civil contractor, at ₹50,600 a tonne delivered on 60-day terms: an invoice of ₹242.88 lakh. The quote was built from the ₹57,500 plate in three steps — 5 per cent for grade and relationship, 4 per cent for lot size, then a flat ₹1,840 a tonne for signing before the mill revision lapsed. The two percentage steps together are 8.8 per cent, not 9; the flat step is 3.2 per cent of plate; the chain lands at exactly 12.00 per cent, the only number in the deal file. Exhibit 3 asks what else it could have been.

Exhibit 4 does the other half. Holding the reference at the plate, it asks what Sauda realised on the same invoice and finds four answers, because four functions net different things out of a delivered, credit-funded, scheme-eligible, ladder-eligible tonne: freight ₹1,450, credit ₹1,122.90, ₹600 to the introducing dealer, ₹950 accruing towards the Loha Ladder.

Jugal Tandi's row will not sit still, because the ₹950 does not yet exist. The ladder pays retroactively on a buyer's whole financial-year offtake: nothing below 1,200 tonnes, ₹450 a tonne from 1,200, ₹950 from 2,500, ₹1,500 from 5,000, credited by end-April. BSP-114 had taken 2,180 tonnes by 30 September, and where it finishes depends on a hospital package it has tendered for. Exhibit 5 prices the endings.

The last piece is structural. Exhibit 6 walks both books from gross value to what Sauda keeps. On the own book, ₹13.94 crore of freight, credit, scheme and accrual joins the ₹36.26 crore of invoice discount, so the value surrendered against plate is ₹50.20 crore, 16.20 per cent, and Exhibit 1's ₹17.34 crore gross margin becomes ₹3.40 crore of contribution. The brokered board has no invoice discount at all: it has ₹0.69 crore of commission Sauda contracted for and did not charge, which sits in revenue, appears in no discount report, and earns the same ₹85 a tonne.

5. The people

Jagriti Dewangan, chief commercial officer, Raipur, owns plate, grid, schemes and ladder, and is measured on margin percentage and revenue growth, which Exhibit 6 shows are not read off the same price. She has not said she doubts her board pack.

Chirag Nirmalkar, national sales head, Bhilai, carries a tonnage target; his realised price is the invoice, because that is what the buyer signs. He is not saying how much September tonnage went to accounts he expects to reach the ₹1,500 slab.

Hulasi Sahu, financial controller, Raipur, built the bridge and signs the covenant certificate; her price nets credit, because she funds it. She is not saying that the two ledgers disagree on the terms of 214 orders.

Champa Bhagel, category manager for cement, Bhopal, prices by district against the grinding units and nets freight and scheme, her levers. She is not saying that her ₹8 a bag scheme was extended without written approval.

Fateh Kurre, head of the Maang Board, Bilaspur, wants the brokered book judged on yield, not discount. He is not saying that he routes marginal own-book enquiries onto the board, which flatters own-book contribution and worsens his own yield.

Jeevika Chandrakar, head of credit and treasury, Raipur, watches receivable days, 60.3 at quarter-end, and wants 90-day terms withdrawn. She is not saying that two of the largest 90-day accounts were her own recommendation.

Jugal Tandi, engagement partner for the statutory auditors, Raipur, holds that the ladder reduces revenue rather than being a marketing cost, and that the accrual must reflect each account's likely finishing slab. He has not said whether he accepts Sauda's forecasts.

Tarek Al Suwaidi, procurement head at Bin Haider Contracting LLC, Sharjah, wants his tonnes priced FOB Paradip by 20 October, in dollars, with no ladder, scheme, credit or freight: the only enquiry with all four deductions stripped out.

6. Voices

"Twelve per cent. The buyer agreed it on the phone, and it is 12.00 per cent of a price we ourselves printed. Everything after that is your cost, not my discount."

Chirag Nirmalkar, pricing call, 7 October

"Then let us print the plate at ₹80,000 and report a 37 per cent discount. The plate is not a price. It is a number we have not revised in eighteen months while our cost moved ₹2,300 a tonne in a fortnight."

Hulasi Sahu, same call

"I have no discount, I have yield: 29,000 tonnes at ₹588 a tonne kept. After Hulasi's deductions I am not persuaded the own book kept more, and we are paid the same ₹85 either way."

Fateh Kurre, chat thread, 9 October

"My question is narrow. At 30 September, what does Sauda expect to pay these accounts in April? If the answer on one account runs from ₹10 lakh to ₹78 lakh, I want to see how the slab was forecast."

Jugal Tandi, limited-review meeting, 9 October

"Ninety days is a discount. We have put it in the interest line where sales cannot see it."

Jeevika Chandrakar, note to Jagriti, 10 October

7. The options as Jagriti sees them

Index the plate. Revise it fortnightly against the mills' circulars and shorten the quote honour to three days. Discount off plate would then mean something stable and Exhibit 2's wandering would stop. It changes nothing in Exhibit 4, and a plate tracking cost makes every negotiation a conversation about Sauda's margin.

Adopt one definition and pay on it. Move the incentive to net realised value as Hulasi computes it, with the ladder accrued at the forecast slab. That gives a single price — and pays the sales team on a forecast that Exhibit 5 puts anywhere in a ₹1,050 band, from ₹450 a tonne to ₹1,500.

Put a floor under the net price. A deal desk: representatives free to ₹49,500 a tonne, Chirag to ₹48,800, anything lower to Jagriti. At a ₹48,800 floor the BSP-114 order clears by ₹1,800 a tonne on Chirag's basis, falls ₹250 short on Champa's, ₹1,372.90 short on Hulasi's. A floor is only as meaningful as its basis.

Separate the books. Judge the Maang Board on yield and the own book on contribution, and pay differently, as Fateh wants. It creates an internal routing price the buyer cannot see.

All four assume the task is to arrive at one authoritative number. Hania's line pointed elsewhere: that the four are true answers to four different questions, and the defect is not their multiplicity but that Sauda has never written down which question each function answers.

8. The deadline and the constraints

The committee sits at nine on Monday 12 October. The covenant on the consortium line requires own-book gross margin of at least 5.0 per cent as reported in the management accounts and receivable days below 68: Exhibit 1 reports 6.34 per cent and the quarter closed at 60.3 days, but Exhibit 6's contribution basis gives 1.31 per cent, and Hulasi signs the certificate by 15 November. Jugal's review closes before the November board, and if he reprices the accrual the covenant margin moves with it. The schemes are contractual for the quarter already run: ₹3.95 crore of payouts and accrual are post-supply, and if the GST position on linking them to invoices is not accepted, up to ₹0.76 crore of tax is not recoverable — ₹0.63 crore on the steel portion at 18 per cent and ₹0.13 crore on the cement portion at 28 per cent. Tarek wants his price by 20 October on a basis no domestic customer uses. And the ladder accrual is only ₹2.31 crore of the ₹13.94 crore between Exhibit 1's ₹17.34 crore and Exhibit 6's ₹3.40 crore, 16.6 per cent, behind the cost of credit at ₹5.87 crore and freight at ₹4.12 crore — but it is the largest item in that gap not yet settled, and becomes a fact only on the last day of March.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what did Sauda discount in the quarter to September 2026? State the figure you would defend and the divisor you used.
  2. Exhibit 3 gives one order four discount depths and Exhibit 4 four realised prices. Which belong in a pricing policy, and which only in a ledger?
  3. The ladder is retroactive to the first tonne. What does that do to the price of a tonne sold in September, and what would a different design do instead?
  4. Commission foregone appears in no discount report. Should a brokered tonne and an own-book tonne earn the same incentive, and what happens to routing if they do not?
  5. Whose definition of realised price should govern the covenant certificate, and whose Chirag's incentive? If they differ, what must be written down?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Jagriti take into the room, what does she refuse to decide before April, and what does she say in November when a director asks how much the company gave away last quarter?

It was past midnight when she closed the laptop. The plate said ₹57,500. The mill said ₹52,400. The rival had said ₹49,800. Somewhere in Bilaspur a contractor was deciding whether to tender for a second hospital package, and the answer would reprice 480 tonnes of steel that had left the yard in September.

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Pricing & Packaging

Discounting and Promotions

When does a discount create value, and when does it train customers to wait? A reading built around one company's quarter-end reflex, and the arithmetic that finally interrupted it.

1 A quarter, three days from closing

On the morning of 27 September 2026, Vignesh Balakrishnan, VP of Growth at Kanivu Vet Systems, opened the pipeline dashboard the way he did every quarter's final week: relief mixed with unease. Kanivu sold cloud practice-management software out of Salem — appointment booking, medical records, billing — to small-animal clinics and animal hospitals across Tamil Nadu, with a growing tail of accounts in Erode and Tiruppur. Fiscal Q2 closed in three days, and the familiar shape had reappeared: a flat first ten weeks, then a wall of signatures crowding the final fortnight. Aravind Krishnamurthy, who ran the Erode-Tiruppur territory, had already messaged twice asking whether the usual 20 percent quarter-end discount on the annual Growth plan was “live yet,” because three clinic owners had told him they were waiting for it.

That sentence was the problem: waiting for it meant the discount no longer closed hesitant deals, it trained patient ones to sit on their hands. Vignesh had run the promotion every quarter for over a year because bookings rose whenever it appeared, but he had never asked what the 20 percent actually bought — new clinics that would not otherwise have signed, or a discount handed to clinics coming anyway, merely later and cheaper. CEO Jayanthi Nair wanted a recommendation before Monday's pricing review: not “run it again” or “cancel it,” but a number showing what the discount had bought, and what a different design would buy instead.

2 The idea, defined plainly

A discount is a temporary reduction from an established list price, offered to change a specific customer's decision — to buy at all, to buy sooner, to buy more, or to buy from you instead of a rival. A promotion is the same lever wrapped in a public, time-boxed frame — a festival sale, a quarter-end offer, a launch price — so the trigger is a date or event rather than a private negotiation. Both are tactics layered on a pricing model (value-based, cost-plus or competitive) this topic assumes is already sound; discounting a badly priced product does not fix the pricing, it hides the symptom.

The logic underneath discounting is old: economist Arthur Pigou described price discrimination — charging different customers different prices for the same good — in the 1920s, later formalised for commercial teams by pricing consultants such as Robert Dolan and Hermann Simon, whose 1996 book Power Pricing treated a discount as an instrument for capturing a segment that would not pay full price, not an apology for the price itself. The sentence Vignesh could repeat without sounding glib: a discount should buy a specific piece of customer behaviour you could not have gotten any other way — never just a lower price for someone already going to pay full freight.

3 The mechanics, step by step

The step practitioners skip is separating list price (the published starting price) from pocket price (what actually lands after every discount and concession on that deal). McKinsey consultants Michael Marn, Eric Roegner and Craig Zawada named the gap between the two the price waterfall: list price flows downward through invoice discounts, payment-term concessions and off-invoice promotions until only the pocket price remains, and it is the pocket price, never list, that determines whether a deal was profitable.

The second, usually implicit, step is asking what the discount is meant to purchase: incremental volume from a customer who would otherwise walk, or accelerated timing from a customer who would otherwise buy in three weeks anyway — identical on an invoice, but different economic events. The third step, which Kanivu had never done systematically, is sorting every discounted deal into one of three buckets after the fact: would have signed anyway, this quarter, at this price; pulled forward from a later quarter; or genuinely incremental. Only the third represents value created; the first is margin surrendered for nothing, and the second is revenue borrowed from a future quarter at a discount.

4 A worked example: the Growth-plan quarter-end promotion

Kanivu's Growth plan, aimed at multi-vet clinics, lists at ₹18,000 per clinic per month, or ₹2.16 lakh a year. Going into the last two weeks of Q2 FY27, 60 clinics sat in the Growth-plan pipeline. Aravind's team, checking CRM history against the previous four quarters, classified them: 25 were tracking to sign this quarter regardless of discount; 11 more were live deals for October or November that a sign-by-30-September offer would plausibly pull forward; and 6 had told reps they were not ready to commit at ₹18,000 but might reconsider at a lower first-year price. All three groups typically convert with the promotion running — 42 of the 60 sign before the quarter closes, since Kanivu had never built a way to offer the discount selectively.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Each discounted clinic gives up ₹3,600 a month, or ₹0.432 lakh across the first year. Multiply by 42 signings and Kanivu hands back ₹18.14 lakh in year-one revenue — but 59.5 percent of that goes to clinics needing no inducement, and a further 26.2 percent buys deals that would have arrived at full price later. Only 14.3 percent is spent on the six clinics the promotion actually recruited. Bookings do rise, from ₹54 lakh with no promotion to ₹72.576 lakh with it — a 34.4 percent jump that looks, on a slide, like the promotion is working.

Now change one input: halve the discount to 10 percent. Judgement, checked against the Q1 FY27 district that ran a smaller promotion, suggests the certain 25 are unaffected, pull-forward shrinks to 8, and the price-sensitive group shrinks to 3, since some of the original six were only over the line at 20 percent.

But the giveaway is only ₹7.78 lakh against ₹18.14 lakh before: less than half the discount for 86 percent of the growth (₹15.98 lakh of ₹18.58 lakh). The lesson is not that smaller discounts are always better; it is that a discount's cost has to be measured against the bucket it funds, not the topline number it sits beside.

5 The nuances a learner must sit with

A discount is not a price cut

A price cut changes the list price for everyone, indefinitely, and belongs in the pricing-model conversation, not this one. A discount is selective and time-bound by design. Once a "temporary" discount has run five consecutive quarters, as Kanivu's had, it has quietly become the real price: every clinic paying list subsidises the ones who waited, and past some threshold — Kanivu was already at 38.1 percent by Q2 FY27 — the published price becomes an opening bid reps expect to be negotiated down.

Discounting is price discrimination, and only works if it discriminates

The economic case for a discount rests on reaching customers who would not otherwise pay, without reaching customers who would. A promotion broadcast to everyone, as Kanivu's was, cannot discriminate; it lands on the certain, the price-sensitive and the fence-sitter alike, which is why 85.7 percent of the Exhibit 2a discount bought nothing incremental.

The three-bucket split is rarely observed directly, but it can be estimated

No CRM field records "would have signed anyway." Kanivu approximated it from deal-stage history and a natural experiment (the Q1 FY27 district that ran a smaller discount); a holdout region that never sees the promotion is the cleanest version of this test.

A discount cannot fix a value problem

If clinics decline because a rival integrates with a lab-diagnostics vendor Kanivu doesn't support, no discount changes that; it only delays the same objection to renewal. Discounting treats price as the friction; sometimes the friction is the product.

Reference prices are sticky, and discounts move them

Behavioural work on anchoring, following Kahneman and Tversky, shows a customer's sense of the "real" price is set by whatever they last paid attention to, not the rate card. A clinic signing at ₹14,400 remembers ₹14,400, and treats full-price renewal as an increase rather than a return to normal.

Governance, not goodwill, keeps discounting disciplined

A deal desk — an approval ladder specifying who may authorise what size of discount — is the difference between discounting with intent and discounting because a rep is one signature short of quota. Kanivu had no ladder; any executive could apply the full 20 percent unilaterally.

6 How this differs by business type and stage

In consumer settings — a pet-food brand selling to the same pet owners Kanivu's clinics serve — discounts are public and mostly harmless, because purchase cycles are short and price memory fades between festival sales. In B2B software like Kanivu's own, each customer remembers their exact number indefinitely, deal cycles run months, and clinic owners compare notes at district veterinary-association meetings, so a discount granted once is effectively granted forever. In a marketplace connecting pet owners to clinics, a discount to one side is usually funded by the other side's take rate, and over-discounting demand can erode supply-side trust. Stage matters too: an early-stage company reasonably discounts heavily for a few marquee reference clinics, since a credible logo's information value can exceed the margin given up; a company at Kanivu's stage faces a stricter test, since every discount is now a precedent a rival such as Kural Practice Cloud can cite.

7 Common mistakes

Reading the quarter-end spike as demand growth. Symptom: a bookings chart that always jumps in the last two weeks. Misunderstanding: treating the jump as demand created rather than demand relocated in time. Diagnostic: compute the "clean quarter" number, bookings excluding the final fortnight; if it is flat while the spike grows, the growth is a scheduling artefact.

Discounting on reflex at the first objection. Symptom: reps offer a discount whenever a prospect hesitates. Misunderstanding: treating every objection as a price objection. Diagnostic: a pass through win-loss notes — if lost deals cite a missing lab integration rather than price, no discount fixes it.

Letting a promotion run indefinitely with no review date. Symptom: nobody remembers why the quarter-end discount started. Diagnostic question: would the company be comfortable if this discount became public and permanent? If yes, it should be the list price; if no, it needs an expiry date and an owner.

8 What good looks like

Picture the same decision handled well a year later. Kanivu still runs a quarter-end offer, but at 10 percent, restricted to single-doctor practices below a stated patient-volume threshold in Erode and Tiruppur, where a controlled test had shown genuine price sensitivity — and any discount above 15 percent anywhere requires deal-desk sign-off. Every quarter, Aravind's team reports three numbers alongside total bookings: the clean-quarter figure, the count of genuinely incremental signings, and the share of the discount pool spent on clinics who would have signed anyway. The promotion still exists, but it is aimed, bounded and reviewed, not a reflex nobody remembers authorising.

9 What Vignesh decided

Vignesh recommended cutting the blanket 20 percent quarter-end discount to 10 percent, restricting eligibility to the price-sensitive segment Exhibit 2b implicitly described, and introducing deal-desk approval for anything larger. Jayanthi approved it for Q3 FY27, with a standing request: report the clean-quarter number every month, so the next review starts from evidence, not the shape of a familiar chart. The reasoning was simple once the buckets were visible — a discount that mostly pays customers who needed no persuading is not a growth lever, it is a tax on the patient, and the fastest way to make more customers patient is to keep paying it.

The natural next reading is on deal desks and discounting exceptions — the governance layer that turns this analysis into a repeatable process — followed by discount architecture, which asks how to design the ladder itself. Two questions worth sitting with: if your least price-sensitive customers discovered exactly what your newest customer paid, would this quarter's discount survive the conversation? And what evidence would convince you a discount bought a customer who would not otherwise exist, rather than one you were always going to keep?

Paimaana Credit Systems: What Did the Increase Actually Do?

An eleven per cent list rise, four realised rises, and a board meeting on Monday morning

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 4 October 2026, Poornima Hegde sat at her dining table in Tumakuru with four printed pages before her, each carrying a different number for the same thing. The board of Paimaana Credit Systems met at half past nine the next morning; the second item read Realised effect of the October 2025 price revision.

Fourteen months earlier the board had approved an eleven per cent rise in the list price of the licence and of the per-application origination fee, effective 1 October 2025, with the per-presentation e-mandate fee held flat. Hegde had drafted that proposal herself. The four pages were honest attempts to say what it had achieved: 5.08 per cent, 4.38 per cent, 3.50 per cent, and one saying the question could not be answered before the end of March.

Beside them lay a message from Vasanth Byrappa, the chief financial officer, sent at nine that evening: Whatever you present, please present one number. Jayanth will ask for one number.

2. The company, and the clause that will not go away

Paimaana was founded in Tumakuru in March 2016 by Jayanth Puttaswamy, who had spent eleven years implementing core banking systems for district co-operative banks that treated loan origination as an afterthought. Paimaana Origination captures an application, runs it through a configurable decisioning workflow, pulls bureau and account-aggregator data and books the sanction; Paimaana Collect presents e-mandates on the NACH rails and runs delinquency queues. By September 2026 it served 240 lenders — 138 urban and district co-operative banks, 102 NBFCs — on annual recurring revenue of ₹37.94 crore: ₹20.36 crore licence, ₹17.58 crore per-transaction.

The decision that shapes what Hegde can do was taken in 2018, and for a good reason. To win the first thirty-eight co-operative banks, Puttaswamy signed contracts with no escalation clause at all: bank boards, he argued, do not sign documents letting a vendor raise its own price. For nine of them — the largest, whose chairmen introduced the rest — he also accepted a most-favoured-customer clause. If Paimaana grants a comparable customer a better effective rate, those nine are entitled to it, backdated over the contract year then running.

Two later corrections complicated the estate rather than simplifying it. In 2020 the standard contract acquired a fixed annual step of four per cent, to look predictable to bank boards. In February 2023, after a federation's auditor objected, the template capped the annual increase at the change in the consumer price index. From January 2025 contracts carried an uncapped clause with ninety days' notice. Four vintages now live side by side (Exhibit 1).

3. The industry

The market has been reshaped twice in five years and almost none of the reshaping was about price. The Reserve Bank of India's four-tiered framework for urban co-operative banks tightened capital and reporting expectations and pushed a wave of amalgamations; three of Paimaana's customers ceased to exist as separate entities inside the measurement window. The digital lending guidelines of 2022 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 forced rework of disclosure, settlement and consent across every lender on the platform. NPCI's e-mandate and UPI Autopay rails made per-presentation pricing a commodity.

The competition is not one kind of company. Lenders running Infosys Finacle or TCS BaNCS can extend those platforms rather than buy an origination system; specialist lending-software firms and analytics layers such as Perfios and Signzy sit in the middle; at the bottom sit spreadsheets and a bank's own IT committee. Paimaana's answer has always been that four years of decisioning rules, audit trails and NACH registrations do not move cheaply.

Two foreign dependencies matter. Paimaana embeds a decisioning rules engine licensed from Avonmead Decision Systems of Bristol at ₹340.00 lakh a year, paid in pounds. And in July 2026 it signed a letter of intent with a Riyadh consumer-finance company whose head of collections, Majed Al Rubaie, agreed a riyal rate card benchmarked to the Indian list price — which is why list price is not an internal fiction.

4. What happened, in order

In April 2025 Hegde and Byrappa built the case on three observations: list price had not moved in three years, delivery cost per account had risen, and the per-application fee sat below what the market appeared to bear. The board approved eleven per cent on 14 August 2025 and the rate card changed on 1 October. Eleven per cent, it was assumed, would arrive net of churn over twelve months.

The first thing to go wrong was visible by December. Deepthi Honnappa, the revenue-operations analyst in Kolar, built a reconciliation ledger called Jodi that joined every contract's escalation clause to every invoice line. Raising Prices Without a Churn Spike

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation — Pricing & Packaging

1. A line on the P&L that would not move

On the second Monday of September 2026, Parminder Deswal sat in her glass-walled office above the operations floor of Lohyantra Fleet Exchange, in Panipat's Model Town, staring at a spreadsheet row that refused to improve no matter how she rearranged the columns around it. Lohyantra ran a marketplace and fleet-management platform called Fleet Cockpit, used by owners of excavators, concrete pumps and boom lifts across Haryana, Punjab and Delhi-NCR to list machines to contractors, track utilisation by GPS, and get paid automatically instead of chasing cheques. By that September, 1,240 fleet owners paid a monthly subscription for Fleet Cockpit, covering 7,400 tagged machines, at a flat ₹1,400 per machine per month, unchanged since launch. Monthly recurring revenue from the tier stood at ₹1,03,60,000, or ₹103.6 lakh.

The row that would not move was margin. Over the preceding year, cost per machine had climbed steadily: the SIM and telematics data behind the GPS tracking, a new AI-based predictive-maintenance feature given free to every subscriber, and a support desk now fielding calls in three languages. Parminder had a board meeting in three weeks and a decision to make: raise the price, and risk the very thing that made Fleet Cockpit valuable — enough machines listed that contractors kept coming back — or hold the price and watch margin keep falling.

2. The idea, in one sentence

A price increase is a deliberate, announced rise in what customers pay for a materially unchanged product, made to capture value it already delivers — distinct from repackaging, where you charge more because you deliver more, and distinct from silently letting margin erode. Alfred Marshall gave economics the concept of price elasticity of demand in 1890: a price change causes a predictable, measurable change in quantity sold. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's 1979 work on loss aversion explained what Marshall's arithmetic alone could not: a rise is felt as a loss against a reference point, so identical rupee amounts land differently depending on how they arrive. Subscription-pricing researchers such as Patrick Campbell, writing in the 2010s, turned both into the playbook most SaaS and marketplace businesses now use: grandfather the existing base, telegraph the change well in advance, and measure what actually happens. The sentence Parminder could repeat in the boardroom without sounding glib: "We are not asking today's customers to pay more for the same thing overnight — we are pricing new customers at what the product is worth now, and giving existing customers a fair, telegraphed path to the same place."

3. How the increase is actually built

The mechanics start where most managers skip: the unit-economics table, not a round percentage. Parminder's colleague Uday Kadyan, who ran data and analytics for Lohyantra out of Hisar, rebuilt the cost per machine for September 2025 and September 2026 before anyone discussed a number.

Table 1 — Fleet Cockpit cost per machine per month

The telematics line alone had risen 21.1% (₹380 to ₹460) as the SIM aggregator repriced data plans; the AI feature added a cost line that had not existed a year before. Total cost per machine was up 38.4% against a price that had not moved, and margin had compressed by exactly 20 points — 47.9% to 27.9%. That table, not a competitor's price list or a feel for "what the market will bear," justified opening the conversation at all.

Once the cost picture justified a rise, three choices followed. First, the increase split in two: a new-customer price, effective immediately, and a smaller grandfathered price for the existing base, phased in only at each owner's renewal — Fleet Cockpit contracts locked the rate for a year, so renewals, not one calendar date, are where the increase lands. Second, comms tiered by account size: plain email for small owners, a call from a named account manager for larger fleets, including a 14-machine contractor in Rohtak named Puneet Rathi. Third — the step practitioners most often skip — the rollout was designed, before a notice went out, to produce a natural experiment: renewal dates already staggered owners across the calendar, so the September and October 2026 cohorts could receive two comms treatments and be compared, rather than treating the whole base as one event.

4. The worked example, and what changes when comms do

Cohort A — 210 owners renewing in September — got the plain-email treatment Lohyantra had always used. Cohort B — 195 owners renewing in October — got an in-app banner showing utilisation savings from the AI feature, plus an account-manager call above ten machines. Uday's team had already established, from eight prior months of renewal cohorts, a baseline churn rate of 3.0% at renewal, for reasons unrelated to price.

Cohort A: 14 of the 210 owners cancelled at renewal, a churn rate of 6.7% — 3.7 points above the 3.0% baseline. Cohort B: 7 of the 195 owners cancelled, a rate of 3.6% — only 0.6 points above baseline. Holding price constant, the only difference between the cohorts was comms, worth 3.1 points of churn on its own.

Carrying Cohort B's 0.6-point excess-churn rate across the full 7,400-machine base — assuming owners who cancel are of average fleet size, so the same percentage applies to machines as to logos — gives 44 machines lost (7,400 × 0.6%, rounded down), leaving 7,356 on the platform at the grandfathered ₹1,570, a 12.1% rise on ₹1,400 (against ₹1,650, a 17.9% rise, for fresh sign-ups). The second pass asks what happens if Lohyantra had rolled the plain-email comms out company-wide instead — Cohort A's 3.667-point excess churn applied everywhere, costing 271 machines (7,400 × 3.667%, rounded down), leaving 7,129.

Run the arithmetic backwards and excess churn would need to reach about 10.8% of the base before the revenue gain vanished, and past 30% before the margin gain did — several multiples worse than the plain-email cohort produced. That cushion, not optimism, let Parminder recommend the increase with confidence.

5. What a learner has to become aware of

Grandfathering needs a sunset, not a permanent exemption. A rate never revisited becomes a second, shrinking price list a company must maintain forever, and every future increase then solves the same problem twice. Good grandfathering states, at the outset, when the legacy rate itself will move.

A price rise cannot repair broken unit economics on its own. If cost per unit already exceeds even the new price, raising price only slows the bleeding; the cost side needs its own fix. Parminder's table still showed a healthy 35.7% margin at the grandfathered rate because the increase and the cost problem were sized together, not chosen independently.

This is not surge pricing. Dynamic, algorithmic repricing of a marketplace transaction serves a different psychological contract: customers expect a transaction price to move with demand, but expect a quoted subscription rate to hold until they are told otherwise.

Low churn after a rise does not prove the new price is right. It tells you how much resistance you met, not whether the product is still underpriced relative to what it delivers; Lohyantra could clear this exercise with 0.6% excess churn and still be leaving value uncaptured.

Ask what "churn" is actually counting. Logo churn (owners) and revenue churn (rupees) can disagree sharply — a rise safe on a logo basis can still be dangerous if the accounts who leave are the biggest ones, why Puneet Rathi's account got a phone call, not an email.

Separate excess churn from baseline churn. Conflating the two either paralyses a company never at risk, or hides a real problem inside a baseline already drifting for unrelated reasons, such as a slow construction season.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

In a consumer subscription, the base is large and cheap per account, so grandfathering is usually one flat legacy price before a cut-off date, and size-based comms tiering means nothing since no consumer account is meaningfully bigger than another. Lohyantra's B2B sale to fleet owners is the opposite: a few hundred accounts of wildly different size, renewing on staggered anniversaries, where one large account's departure can outweigh a hundred small ones — why size-based tiering did the real work in Section 4. The marketplace layer adds something neither pure model considers: raising what owners pay changes what contractors experience too, since fewer listed machines means thinner search results and a chance contractors drift to a rival aggregator — the customer to watch is not only the one notified. An early-stage Lohyantra, with perhaps forty owners in 2020, would have had neither enough accounts for a meaningful control cohort nor the buffer to risk losing a few marquee ones, so it would more plausibly have negotiated price account-by-account; the staggered design only works once the base and renewal calendar are large enough to produce two comparable cohorts.

7. Where this goes wrong

Announcing one flat rise for everyone, with no grandfathering. The symptom is a spike in cancellations at the next renewal window, disproportionately among the longest-tenured accounts. The error is treating existing and new customers as identical, when existing customers formed their willingness to pay under the old price and feel any change as a loss. The cheapest diagnostic: split last year's churn by tenure first — if long-tenured accounts already churn less, a flat rise lands hardest where it can least be afforded.

Skipping the control group. The symptom is a team that blames every cancellation next quarter on the price change, including ones tied to an unrelated seasonal slowdown. The error is mistaking total post-increase churn for the churn the increase caused. The cheapest diagnostic: find any stagger already built into the billing calendar — renewal month, region, plan tier — and compare a not-yet-treated group before concluding anything.

Choosing the percentage before the cost math. The symptom is a number nobody on the account team can defend on a call — "why 15%, why not 10%?" The error is treating the increase as a negotiating gambit rather than the output of a table like Uday's. The cheapest diagnostic: ask whoever announces the figure to recite what it does to margin per unit; if they cannot, it was chosen for optics, not economics.

8. What good looks like

Good looks like exactly what Cohort B produced, rolled out to the whole base: a grandfathered rate reaching owners only at renewal, a phone call instead of an email where it mattered, a rise justified by a cost table anyone could recite, and a control group built in from day one rather than assembled after a bad quarter. The result: MRR of ₹115.49 lakh against ₹103.6 lakh before, margin up 42.7%, and 7,356 of the original 7,400 machines still listed — liquidity barely dented. Puneet Rathi renewed without complaint; the account-manager call had made the AI feature visible as worth paying for, price aside.

9. What Parminder decided, and what to sit with next

Parminder took the board a recommendation built from the table, not the calendar: ₹1,650 for new customers, ₹1,570 for the existing base phased in at renewal, sixty days' notice, comms tiered by fleet size, and a rollback trigger if excess churn in any future cohort crossed roughly twice Cohort B's rate. Her reasoning was the arithmetic itself — a rise that still added margin under a churn assumption several times worse than anything observed. What she flagged to learn next was pricing power as a moat: today proved Lohyantra could raise price once without damage; whether it can do so again next year without owners or contractors walking is a harder, ongoing question, tied to repackaging and tier migration — charging more for more, rather than more for the same. Two questions worth sitting with: if Cohort B's excess churn had matched Cohort A's, would the same breakeven arithmetic still have said "raise the price" — and whose churn should a fleet-management marketplace watch first, the owner who received the notice, or the contractor who never received one at all?

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

A price increase is a deliberate, announced rise in the tariff charged for a product whose delivered value has not changed in the same step. The narrowness is the point: it excludes repackaging, a new value metric, and indexation clauses that fire automatically. What is left is the hard case — asking someone to pay more for what they have.

The history runs along two tracks that met late. The economic track begins with Arthur Cecil Pigou's 1920 taxonomy of price discrimination, which established that a single price is a choice rather than a fact; measurement followed, with André Gabor and Clive Granger's survey technique in the mid-1960s and Peter van Westendorp's Price Sensitivity Meter in 1976. The behavioural track begins with Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler's 1986 work on fairness as a constraint on profit seeking. Their finding, dual entitlement, is that customers grant the firm a right to its reference profit and themselves a right to their reference price: they accept a rise that shields the firm's margin from a cost shock and punish an identical one framed as opportunism. The justification, not the magnitude, decides.

Thomas Nagle and Reed Holden's The Strategy and Tactics of Pricing (1987) and Hermann Simon's work on price management welded the tracks into practice; Madhavan Ramanujam's Monetizing Innovation (2016) pushed further. Four camps now disagree substantively.

The sharpest split is between the fairness and value-capture schools. The first says a rise is safe only when the customer can see the cost behind it; the second says that reasoning teaches customers your margin is their business, and that the durable instrument is a contractual escalator agreed once at signature. The repackaging school refuses the premise: if you cannot deliver more, do not charge more.

3. Mechanics: from the announcement to the cash

Most of expert practice happens before a number is chosen. Wamsi Bommireddy, Gavaksha's head of data science in Anantapur, spent six weeks on an estimate of the demand curve, a segmentation of the base by cost to serve, and an audit of the payment rails. Teams skip the first, believing price cannot be tested under contract. It can — on new customers.

None of which is the number that matters. That is realisation: how much of the rise reaches the bank in year one, given that renewals are spread across the calendar.

Roughly half of an announced increase disappears into the calendar. Boards that congratulate themselves on 12.05 per cent and then find revenue up under 6 per cent are meeting Exhibit 3 for the first time.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Three conditions can be stated as claims checkable before committing; each resolves differently for the two protagonists.

Claim one: breakeven churn is comfortably above anything the business has seen. A 12.05 per cent increase tolerates logo churn, at constant account mix, of 10.76 per cent — one minus the reciprocal of 1.1205. Gavaksha's 0.72 per cent excess churn leaves roughly fifteen times' headroom. Rutuchakra's test differs in kind, because nothing need cancel for revenue to fall: an 18.18 per cent rise breaks even at a 15.38 per cent fall in volume. Usage pricing turns a churn question into a throttling question, and throttling is silent.

Claim two: the value is legible to the payer at the moment of the rise. Tariff Desk publishes a monthly RevPAR comparison against a local competitive set, so an owner sees what the product earned him. Channel Pulse is infrastructure, invisible when working. Legibility governs how hard a rise is to defend, not whether it is deserved. Bhavani's rise was the harder sell for that reason alone.

Claim three: the increase is not doing work that belongs to the cost side. A homestay costs Gavaksha ₹901.60 a month to serve — ₹310 of channel-manager API calls, ₹140 of hosting, ₹186.60 of forecasting inference, ₹265 of allocated support — against ₹2,400 of revenue, a 62.43 per cent gross margin. The rise captured value; it did not repair unit economics. Where cost per unit approaches price, a rise buys time and nothing else.

The idea misleads in two situations: a product whose customers are themselves in a price war, where raising a hotelier's software bill during a collapse in room rates transfers pain rather than sharing it; and a two-sided product, where the customer to model never receives the notice.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product portfolios break the neat story, because a customer sees one invoice. Gavaksha's chain tier bundles Tariff Desk with a reporting add-on at ₹4,000 per property, so an 11.82 per cent rise on the subscription is a 10.00 per cent rise on the customer's bill of ₹26,000 — and the customer will quote whichever number suits.

Rail-mediated environments add a mechanical hazard, as the e-mandate finding showed: the rise must clear the payment instrument before it clears the customer. The GST slab boundary at a ₹7,500 declared room tariff has the same character one level down: Gavaksha's customers price around it, so the product's recommendations must respect a threshold unrelated to demand.

AI-native products put the strain on the cost side. Inference is not uniform across a flat-priced tier: of the 1,120 homestays, the heaviest 112 consumed ₹640 a month of forecasting inference, the next 448 consumed ₹214 and the remaining 560 consumed ₹74, a weighted mean of ₹186.60. Gross margin at ₹2,400 is 62.43 per cent on the average property and 43.54 per cent on a heavy one. A uniform percentage rise preserves that dispersion; only a change of value metric removes it.

At the organisational seams, the reliable failure is that sales compensation is not repriced alongside the product. If quota credit runs on new bookings, save-desk concessions cost the rep nothing, and Gavaksha's 47 concessions become 200 next year. Mature companies call a price increase a marketing exercise; what they run is a compensation-plan change, a billing migration and a staffing plan.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Realisation, not the headline percentage, is the unit of account.
The tell is a pricing memo reporting one number. An expert's reports two — the ladder and the realisation forecast — knowing the second is roughly half the first in year one. That a 12.05 per cent rise yields 12.05 per cent more revenue is wrong for a reason that is purely calendrical.
Grandfathering without a sunset creates a permanent second price list.
The tell is a billing system with more active rate codes than tiers. Gavaksha's notice stated that the grandfathered rate would converge to list at the second renewal after October 2027. Without that sentence every future rise solves this problem twice, and the legacy cohort's expectations harden each year.
Excess churn is the only churn worth arguing about.
The tell is a team quoting post-increase churn with no baseline. Gavaksha's 1.96 per cent was frightening until set against the 1.25 per cent the same window produced a year earlier. A base already drifting hides a real pricing problem inside a number that looks unchanged.
Usage-priced products do not churn; they shrink.
The tell is a retention dashboard that looks perfect while revenue per account slides. Bhavani's 430 properties were all still there in December; what had left was volume. An expert asks for the volume series first and treats a flat logo count as evidence of nothing.
The payment rail is part of the pricing decision.
The tell is that nobody can say what the registered mandate ceiling is. Involuntary churn from a failed auto-debit is indistinguishable in the data from a customer rejecting the price, and the remedy is entirely different. Half of Gavaksha's cancellations came from a re-registration step most teams never model.
Concessions are a policy, not a series of decisions.
The tell is different account managers granting materially different terms in the same week. Gavaksha's save desk had three permitted concessions — a six-month deferral, a one-tier step-down, or a twenty-four-month lock at an intermediate rate — and no authority to invent a fourth. Discretion is how a 12 per cent rise becomes a 7 per cent rise without anyone deciding it should.
Seasonality will lie to you, in whichever direction is most flattering.
The tell is a before-and-after comparison spanning a festival quarter. Rutuchakra's revenue rose 9.41 per cent after the rise, and the correct conclusion was that the rise had destroyed value, because the comparison quarter was the peak. Build the counterfactual before the announcement, not after the result.
Low churn is not evidence that the new price is right.
The tell is a team declaring victory and closing the file. Gavaksha cleared the programme at 0.72 per cent excess churn, consistent with the product having been underpriced by considerably more than 12 per cent. Resistance measures how hard you pushed, not how far you could have.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

Across product types the differences are mechanical. In consumer subscriptions the base is large, homogeneous and reached by one email, so grandfathering is a date rather than a negotiation. In B2B the base is small, heterogeneous and renews on staggered anniversaries, which is what makes Exhibit 3 both possible and necessary. Platforms face the second-side problem: Gavaksha's rise never touches the OTAs whose inventory decides whether the product works. Hardware differs in one respect only — the rise applies to the next unit sold, not to an installed base, so there is nothing to grandfather — and AI products differ in cost dispersion, not in the mechanics of the rise.

Stage changes the instrument, not the logic. At forty customers Gavaksha could not have run a three-arm test and had no staggered calendar; the right move then is to raise the new-customer price and leave the base alone, because the base is the reference list. At tens of thousands of accounts, increases become a standing annual escalator in the contract.

8. Three worked examples

Gandikota Heritage Stays. Latha Yerraguntla ran six properties on the chain tier and asked for a twenty-four-month lock in exchange for paying the term up front. At list her six would pay ₹24,600 for twelve months and an assumed ₹26,600 for twelve more: ₹36.86 lakh. Her lock, ₹23,200 per property per month prepaid, came to ₹33.41 lakh — ₹3.46 lakh, or 9.38 per cent, less, and a rise of only 5.45 per cent on ₹22,000. The save desk approved it: discounted monthly at Gavaksha's 14 per cent cost of capital the list path is worth ₹31.90 lakh today, so the lock was 4.71 per cent more valuable than holding firm.
