It survived narrowly on the arithmetic, and the narrowness is the lesson: it spent a quarter of its base to buy 3.54 per cent of revenue, then gave it back.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The commonest failure is judging the programme on the wrong window. The warning is a revenue chart starting at the announcement rather than the first renewal. The diagnostic question is what share of the base has actually reached its renewal, and caught late this costs a rollback of a price that was working.

The second is the uncontrolled save desk. The warning is concessions rising month on month while objections fall — they are being offered, not requested. The diagnostic is to read ten save-call notes and check whether the customer asked; caught late, the realised ladder sits well below the announced one.

The third is confusing absence of complaint with acceptance. In Indian SME segments customers often do not object; they simply do not re-authorise the mandate. The warning is a re-registration rate below ninety per cent, and the diagnostic is to reconcile billing against subscriptions in the first thirty days.

The fourth is raising price into a customer downturn. The warning is the customers' own metric — for Gavaksha, base RevPAR — falling two quarters running. The diagnostic is whether the bill is a smaller share of the customer's revenue than last year. Caught late, it costs the relationship.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the base be grandfathered at all? The fairness school says yes, resting on dual entitlement: customers who formed their reference price under the old list read a full rise as a violation, and tenure correlates with sensitivity to change rather than to level. The value-capture school says grandfathering is a subsidy to your most loyal customers funded by your newest, and teaches the base to wait; it rests on firms running escalators for decades without incident. For the first to be wrong, tenured customers would have to react no more than new ones; for the second, escalator firms would have to survive on switching costs rather than consent.

Can you experiment on price in B2B? The measurement school tests on new customers, as Gavaksha did, accepting that new customers are not the base. The objection is commercial, not methodological: two prospects in one district discover different quotes. The steelman for refusing is that in a market of 1,940 properties clustered in a few towns, price opacity is unachievable and the reputational cost exceeds the information gained. For that to be wrong, customers would have to read price variation as ordinary practice, which hoteliers might.

Is a pure increase ever the right instrument? The repackaging school's strongest form is not that increases are unfair but that they are wasteful: the same conversation could have carried a new tier, metric or add-on, and you get one such conversation a year. Against it: repackaging carries engineering, migration and sales-training costs a price change does not. For the school to be wrong, the trust spent on a pure rise would have to be worth less than the cost of the packaging change — an empirical question nobody has answered well.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this differs in four ways. They start at the billing system and the renewal calendar rather than the percentage, because those decide what is collectible. They insist on a counterfactual before the announcement, knowing none can be built afterwards. They write the grandfathered rate's sunset into the first notice. And they treat a clean result with suspicion: 0.72 per cent excess churn on a 12.05 per cent rise says where to test next.

12. What the protagonists decided

Lavanya went ahead on 1 November 2026 with the ladder in Exhibit 1: ninety days' notice, the grandfathered rate applying at each property's own renewal, convergence to list at the second renewal after October 2027, three permitted concessions and no others, and a mandate re-registration campaign with its own owner. Her reasoning was the cushion — fifteen times' headroom to breakeven churn — and a forecast telling the board to expect ₹77.59 lakh in year one, not ₹165.60 lakh.

Bhavani did not roll back. She kept ₹13 as the marginal rate and added the platform fee, accepting eight cancellations and a hard conversation about why a quarter that looked like 9.41 per cent growth was reported internally as a ₹2.45 lakh loss.

Discussion questions.

  1. Gavaksha realised 46.85 per cent of the theoretical year-one value of its rise. Is that a well-run programme or a badly designed ladder, and which line of Exhibit 3 would you attack first?
  2. Rutuchakra's logo retention held at 98.14 per cent and the rise still destroyed value. What should Bhavani have instrumented on 1 October that she did not?
  3. Gopuram stayed inside its breakeven churn and still ended below where it started. If breakeven arithmetic did not protect it, what should it have solved for instead?

13. Going deeper

Value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing is the strategy a rise revises; without a view on which you run, a rise is a number without a theory. Renewals, churn and NRR is where increases land and supplies the bridge that says whether the rise paid. Pricing power as the test of a moat asks the harder question Gavaksha now faces: whether it can raise again. Repackaging and tier migration is what Rutuchakra reached for after its failure, and the value metric is what Bhavani got wrong first. When to charge and willingness-to-pay research sit upstream of Exhibit 2; packaging: good / better / best gives a rise somewhere to hide; freemium vs free trial decides whether a trial-to-paid test exists at all; what pricing signals closes the loop.

Ikaai Lab Cloud: Raising Prices on an Installed Base

A decision case on grandfathering, communication and measuring churn

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Ishwari Poojary, chief product officer of Ikaai Lab Cloud, sat in the company's fourth-floor office in Mangaluru with a single slide open on her screen. The slide carried one sentence from the chief executive, Charith Shetty: "Bring the board a price change we can defend by the fifteenth." The board would meet in nine days. Ikaai had not raised list price in three and a half years.

Poojary had two drafts on her desk. The finance draft raised every customer's monthly platform fee by 12 per cent at once. Beside it her customer-success colleagues had scribbled one word, "Udupi", where a cluster of small collection-centre labs had told them, not gently, what they thought of the last increase.

2. Company background

Ikaai Lab Cloud sells a laboratory information system (LIS) to pathology and diagnostic laboratories. The software tracks a sample from collection to report, manages analyser interfaces, issues signed reports and keeps the audit trail that an NABL assessor expects to see when a lab is assessed against ISO 15189. Founded in 2016, it grew from a one-lab pilot in Mangaluru to 1,240 paying laboratories across Karnataka, Kerala, Gujarat and Maharashtra.

Pricing follows the pattern of the market: a monthly platform fee per lab, plus per-report slabs that fall as volume rises. Prices are quoted before 18 per cent GST. It competes with a handful of regional LIS vendors, with billing tools stretched to cover lab work, and, for the largest chains, with in-house systems of the kind national names such as Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis and Thyrocare are known to run. Its pitch is that a lab with years of NABL-ready records does not want to move them.

3. The situation

Three pressures had converged. First, Ikaai's annual delivery cost, covering cloud hosting, support and licences, stood at ₹4.20 crore against annual revenue of ₹11.11 crore. Aino Virtanen, the account manager at the Helsinki-based vendor whose analyser-interface middleware Ikaai licenses in euros, had confirmed a 9 per cent rise from January. Ikaai expected delivery cost to rise by that 9 per cent, to ₹4.578 crore, taking gross margin from 62.2 per cent to 58.8 per cent if prices stayed put.

Second, the product had improved. It had added ABDM-linked report sharing and DPDP Act consent records since 2023. The price had not moved to reflect them.

Third, the last increase was a warning. In April 2023 Ikaai raised platform fees by 8 per cent for everyone, on one email, on one date. Exhibit 2 shows what followed. Ishani Kulal, head of customer success, still keeps the replies.

Distance shaped how people read the problem. In Helsinki, Virtanen saw a simple cost pass-through. In Surat, the sales lead saw chains that compare Ikaai against in-house builds every renewal. In Kozhikode, Kulal saw owners who read a platform fee as a personal tax.

4. The people

Ishwari Poojary (Mangaluru), chief product officer and the decision owner, wants an increase that restores margin without giving competitors an opening.

Omkar Bhandary (Mangaluru), chief financial officer, wants the full 12 per cent on all customers, at once. His point: the cost rise arrives in January regardless.

Ishani Kulal (Kozhikode), head of customer success, owns the renewal relationships. She wants small labs shielded and fears a blanket notice will be read as betrayal.

Upendra Ballal (Surat), sales lead for chains, argues that the large accounts are the least price-sensitive and the most valuable, and will accept a rise explained in terms of audit and uptime.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows the installed base. Ikaai has three tiers. Tier A is the collection-centre plan, Tier B the standard laboratory plan and Tier C the multi-site chain plan. Tiers B and C hold 720 of the 1,240 labs but ₹56,00,000 of the ₹69,00,000 monthly platform revenue, and Tier B alone contributes about 49 per cent of annual revenue.

6. The options

Option A: 12 per cent on every lab, at once. Every customer receives notice and the new fee applies mid-term where contracts allow. The upside is speed. Applying the Exhibit 2 excess-churn assumptions, about 47 Tier A and 17 Tier B labs would leave.

Option B: hold list prices. This avoids any churn risk and keeps goodwill, but with the January cost rise gross margin falls from 62.2 per cent to 58.8 per cent.

Tiers B and C take the 12 per cent at each lab's renewal date, after a written 90-day notice signed by Shetty that lists the features added since 2023 and offers a free NABL audit-trail export. New customers pay the new list price at once. The cost is a slower ramp. 7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which tiers carry Ikaai's revenue, and which carry its churn risk? Why do they differ?
  2. In Exhibit 3, Tier A contributes ₹17.03 lakh of uplift and loses ₹17.48 lakh of revenue under Option A. What does that imply about raising its price now?
  3. What does Option B cost, and when would holding prices be right?

8. A note for the learner

The lens of this topic is that a price rise on an installed base is a retention problem before it is a revenue problem. Three ideas frame it: who is grandfathered and for how long, how the increase is communicated, and how churn is measured against a baseline. Renewal is where an increase lands most fairly.

One defensible path is Option C, with sharper conditions. Its reasoning runs as follows. Apply the increase to Tiers B and C, where the evidence shows low price sensitivity and where most revenue sits. Hold Tier A, where at 12 per cent the assumed 9-point excess churn costs ₹3,348 a lab against ₹3,276 gained, a net loss of ₹72. Give 90 days' written notice and tie the message to audit-trail value, not to inflation. Apply it at renewal.

Option C wins even when its churn assumption is challenged. If Tier B lost 3 points, as in Option A, 17 labs would leave and the net run-rate would be ₹62.52 lakh, still above Option A's ₹62.07 lakh, with far less relationship damage. The main risk is the ramp: only about ₹37.1 lakh arrives in year one, against a cost rise of ₹37.8 lakh.

Measure the outcome each month, not once a year. Track renewals by tier against the baseline of 5 per cent annual churn in Tier B and 2 per cent in Tier C. If Tier B excess churn exceeds 2 points, the level seen in 2023, pause the rollout and revisit. Poojary would take this plan to the board on 15 October and ask Bhandary to accept a slower ramp for lower risk.

Nikhar Ceramic Industries: What Does a Tile Cost?

An ambiguous case on value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Nirali Sorathiya was still in the sample room at Morbi with forty-eight tiles on the floor. All the same tile: an 800 by 1600 millimetre glazed vitrified slab in warm grey marble print, the first product of Nikhar Ceramic Industries' new large-format line, the range it calls Eshanya. In the morning she had to put a number on it.

The number was due at nine; the dealer circular went to the printers on Friday, 20 November. Nirali, General Manager, Products, had spent five weeks on evidence meant to settle the question, and it had not narrowed. Her costing sheet gave the cost of one square metre of Eshanya as anything between ₹172.56 and ₹454.27, every figure in that range carrying the signature of someone she respected. The competitor's price had turned out to be five figures. And the person who admired the tile most was not the one who would pay for it.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2019

Nikhar was founded in 2006 in Morbi by Ekansh Jethva's father, as most of the cluster was: one wall-tile kiln, a family guarantee against the term loan, a body-preparation unit at Wankaner. By 2026 it ran four lines and sold ₹427 crore of tiles in the year to March 2026, a middle-sized unit among some 700 factories, none with a brand of its own.

The decision that shaped everything came in March 2019, when Nikhar agreed to manufacture on an outsourcing basis for two national tile brands. The agreements pay audited cost plus 14 per cent, and the contract defines cost: full absorption of variable and fixed cost, with fixed cost divided by rated capacity rather than actual output. The promoter accepted it because the old lines then ran near capacity. Seven years later that work is 62 per cent of revenue, and Nikhar's binding, audited answer to "what does a tile cost" does not agree with the one its own finance department uses for its own brand. Both are correct; they were built to do different jobs.

The Eshanya line is the attempt to stop being only a contract manufacturer. The board approved it in August 2023: ₹148 crore of capital expenditure, ₹132 crore plant and kiln and ₹16 crore land and building. It fires a nominal 12,000 square metres a day over 330 days — a rated 39.60 lakh square metres a year — and cannot be switched off without losing refractory life.

3. The industry

Indian tile output is concentrated in Morbi to a degree with few parallels in Indian manufacturing, and the cluster supplies the market two ways at once: under its own modest brands, and as the manufacturing base for national brands such as Kajaria and Somany. A Morbi unit competes with its own customers in the same lists.

Three forces sit on the price. Gas is the largest input, supplied through Gujarat Gas, its transmission element moving on the orders of the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board. Size is the second: the Bureau of Indian Standards governs what may be sold as vitrified under IS 15622, but nothing governs what size a unit presses, and when 800 by 1600 began to sell in 2024 more than forty units installed presses within eighteen months. Trade is the third: India carries anti-dumping duties on Chinese tiles, and European buyers have brought proceedings whose arithmetic compares the export price with the price the same producer charges at home — so a high domestic price is not a purely domestic fact. Asian Paints sells adhesives into the same projects, but it is the builder's purchase officer who issues the order.

The line first fired in June 2024 and gave 71 per cent firsts. Nayan Khachar rebuilt the sorting line with an engineer from the kiln supplier in Castellon, and by March 2026 yield had settled at 82 per cent firsts, 13 per cent commercial seconds and 5 per cent scrap, four points short of the note. The plan for the year to March 2028 assumes 24.00 lakh square metres fired, not 28.00 lakh, because the contract work needs the line too.

The price assumption failed differently. The circular prints on Friday, 20 November, and 340 dealers with no November list buy somebody else's tile through the season. The Hamburg confirmation lapses on 30 November. Value-Based, Cost-Plus and Competitive Pricing

Should a price anchor on what something is worth, what it costs, or what rivals charge — and how does a product leader know which one to trust this quarter?

1. A Tuesday in Vadodara

On the morning of 22 September 2026, Ojas Thacker opened a spreadsheet he had been avoiding for three weeks. As head of pricing and monetisation at Nakshatra Vivah Exchange (NVE), a wedding-and-event marketplace matching families in Vadodara, Anand and Nadiad to venues, caterers, decorators, make-up artists and photographers, Ojas faced a simple question: what should the platform charge a wedding photographer for featured placement, and was the eighteen-month-old number anywhere close to right.

NVE runs on two revenue lines common to a two-sided marketplace: an 8 per cent take rate on bookings a family confirms in-app, and a monthly subscription vendors buy for visibility — three tiers named Chandan (free), Kesar (mid, featured placement and a badge) and Kundan (top, a homepage banner and relationship manager). Across NVE's 480 photographer accounts, Kesar had been priced at launch by adding a margin to serving cost, and nobody had revisited it since. With the November wedding season approaching, Ojas needed a renewal price by Friday, when Yamini Sanghani, NVE's CEO, wanted the recommendation.

What made the Tuesday uncomfortable was a rumour from a vendor WhatsApp group: photographers were comparing Kesar unfavourably with what a rival, Nutan Utsav Cloud, charged for a similar "Spotlight" badge. Raise the price and guess wrong, and NVE risked an exodus before the season that funds most of a photographer's year; leave it alone, and NVE was likely leaving a large sum on the table monthly. The spreadsheet was, in effect, a test of which anchor — cost, competitors, or value — applied here.

2. The idea: three anchors for one number

A pricing anchor is the evidence a team uses to decide what to charge, and practitioners reach for one of three. Cost-plus pricing adds a target margin to what it costs to produce and deliver the offering — the oldest and most mechanical of the three, inherited from cost-accounting practice that hardened into standard manufacturing use through the early twentieth century. Competitive pricing sets the price by reference to what comparable rivals charge, formalised as a strategic category in marketing texts from the 1960s onward, and rooted in the oligopoly models of economists such as Joseph Bertrand, who showed a firm rarely prices in isolation from rivals. Value-based pricing sets the price by the economic value the offering creates for the customer, sharpened in industrial marketing during the 1980s through the "economic value to the customer" work of McKinsey's John Forbis and Nitin Mehta, later systematised by Thomas Nagle and Reed Holden.

Each anchor solves a different problem: cost-plus for survival, never pricing below what it costs to exist; competitive pricing for credibility, staying inside the range buyers consider normal; value-based pricing for the harder question neither other anchor touches — how much of the customer's benefit the seller may keep. The sentence Ojas could repeat without sounding glib: cost tells you the floor, competitors tell you the neighbourhood, value tells you the ceiling — the price itself is a judgment inside that band, not the output of one formula.

3. How the three anchors are actually built

Building a cost-plus floor starts with isolating the marginal cost of one more account — for Kesar, hosting and ranking-algorithm compute plus a slice of support time, costed by NVE's finance lead, Yash Vekaria in Mumbai, at ₹1,400 per photographer per month. A standard 40 per cent margin gives a floor of ₹1,400 ÷ 0.60 = ₹2,333 — a number practitioners often stop at, mistaking a floor for an answer.

Building a competitive anchor means finding a genuinely comparable offer and asking what it costs and why. Nutan Utsav Cloud's Spotlight badge, the one photographers cited, was priced at ₹6,500 a month — real, but reflecting Nutan's own cost base and delivered lift, not NVE's.

Building a value-based ceiling is the step teams usually leave implicit, since it requires a causal claim: how much more revenue does featured placement put in a vendor's pocket, above what they would have earned anyway? That needs a measurable proxy — leads received and the share converting into a booking — captured before and after upgrade, isolated from the seasonal upswing. Only with that pair can a team compute the value added, which is the arithmetic Ojas ran next.

4. The arithmetic Ojas actually ran

Ojas pulled six months of data for photographers who had upgraded to Kesar and compared their funnel before and after. A typical Vadodara photographer on Chandan received 14 leads a month at 12 per cent conversion, giving 14 × 0.12 = 1.68 bookings a month. After upgrading, leads rose to 21 — a 50 per cent lift — conversion held at 12 per cent, giving 21 × 0.12 = 2.52 bookings, up 0.84. At an average Vadodara wedding-photography booking of ₹85,000, gross booking value rose from 1.68 × ₹85,000 = ₹1,42,800 to 2.52 × ₹85,000 = ₹2,14,200 — an incremental ₹71,400 a month from Kesar alone.

5. Six nuances a learner must sit with

Selection can masquerade as lift

The 50 per cent lead increase assumes Kesar caused it. It is equally plausible that photographers already improving — better portfolios, faster replies — are the ones who upgrade. Without a comparison against vendors who did not, "value created" risks describing selection, not causation.

Cost-plus is a floor, never an answer

NVE's original ₹2,499 price was set almost exactly by cost-plus logic — 7 per cent above the ₹2,333 floor. That protects margin but says nothing about worth; a floor mistaken for a strategy quietly under-prices everything it touches.

A rival's price answers "what's normal," not "what's fair here"

Matching Nutan's ₹6,500 outright would have priced Kesar at just 9.1 per cent of the value it demonstrably creates (₹6,500 ÷ ₹71,400) — below the rate NVE chose, since Nutan's delivered lift and cost base are not NVE's.

A value ceiling is approached cautiously, not hit

Pricing at the full ₹10,710 that 15 per cent capture implies works arithmetically but invites two risks: vendors comparing notes at trade meets feeling extracted from, and a renewal next year with no room to move. Pricing below the ceiling is a decision, not a failure of nerve.

Value and elasticity are different axes

A photographer may agree the lift is worth ₹71,400 and still resist paying ₹7,999 upfront, since vendor income mostly arrives after the event, in a lump, while the subscription bills monthly through a lean pre-season. Willingness to pay and ability to pay are not the same fact.

The three anchors triangulate; they do not vote

None of cost, competitors or value is "more correct." A team asking only one question misprices predictably — cost-only under-prices growth features, competitor-only imports a rival's mistakes, value-only risks a story the market has not accepted.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

A pure consumer app usually has thin per-user value data and leans on competitive anchoring by default — a family choosing between two wedding-planning apps rarely lets a firm run a pricing experiment on them. A B2B seller often has exactly what value-based pricing needs: a named buyer, a measurable outcome, a conversation where the seller walks through arithmetic line by line, as Ojas did with Yamini. A marketplace like NVE sits in between, needing a different anchor on each side — value logic for vendors who see their own funnel, competitive anchoring for the family-facing take rate, where users rarely compare price.

Scale changes which anchor a team can attempt. An early-stage marketplace with a few dozen vendors has no reliable before-and-after data and is forced toward cost-plus or a guessed match. NVE, three years in with clean records, had what a value calculation needs: enough vendors, enough history, a payments trail making "before and after" measurable. The lesson — three anchors, and knowing when each dominates — is a claim about evidence: use the one whose evidence you have.

7. Common mistakes

Pricing nationally when value is local

Symptom: one number rolled out everywhere, adoption weakening outside the biggest city. Misunderstanding: treating an average incremental value as valid everywhere. Diagnostic: recompute value using the local deal size, as Section 4's second pass did.

Setting a price once and never re-checking it

Symptom: a fee unmoved since launch even as the product improved. Misunderstanding: cost-plus was correct at launch, nobody re-asked afterward. Diagnostic: recompute price ÷ measured value on a fixed schedule; a falling ratio is silent under-pricing.

Confusing a stated price with a willingness to pay it

Symptom: a survey asks what vendors would pay, price is set at the average answer, renewals collapse. Misunderstanding: a stated number and one a vendor renews at, once real leads show, differ. Diagnostic: run the price as a measured trial before locking it, as Section 8 describes.

8. What good looks like

Before recommending a number, Ojas ran a six-week trial across upgrading photographers, split by city tier, and waited a full booking cycle to remeasure lift rather than trust the historical average outright. Only once ₹7,999 and ₹5,499 held up under fresh measurement did he bring them to Yamini and Yash for sign-off, floor, rival price and ceiling shown on one page — a judgment inside a band, not a guess dressed as a formula.

Photographer subscription revenue rises from ₹7.07 lakh to ₹14.95 lakh a month, up 111 per cent — and the Vadodara Kesar price still leaves roughly a quarter of its ₹10,710 value ceiling unclaimed.

9. What Ojas decided, and two questions

Ojas recommended the split price, and stopping short of full value capture on purpose. Cost said he could not go below ₹2,333; Nutan said ₹6,500 was already normal to vendors who compare notes; the funnel data said the feature was worth up to ₹10,710 in Vadodara and ₹7,308 in Anand/Nadiad. Roughly 11 per cent capture in both places kept NVE above its floor, above its rival, and visibly short of the ceiling — built to survive the vendor WhatsApp group's scrutiny before the season NVE most needed those photographers to stay.

The natural next step is asking what happens when NVE moves this price again next year — raising prices without the cover of "we underpriced it," and pricing psychology, since a second increase lands differently than the first. Sit with two questions: if the algorithm lifts leads a further 20 per cent, should the price rise automatically, or must someone decide that on purpose? And when the anchors disagree this much — a ₹2,333 floor, a ₹6,500 market number, a ₹10,710 ceiling — whose evidence carries the most weight: the cost sheet, the rival's price list, or the vendor's own booking calendar?

Sthaayi EV Works: Pricing the Shikhar

A decision case on value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing

1. Opening

On the evening of Thursday, 15 October 2026, Bhuvana Alagappan stood at the window of the product office in Hosur and watched the second shift file into the plant. She was Chief Product Officer of Sthaayi EV Works, and on Monday, 19 October, she had to tell the leadership committee what the company's first premium electric scooter, the Shikhar, should cost. Dealer price lists were due at the printers on Tuesday. Deepavali fell on 8 November, the busiest fortnight of the year for two-wheeler showrooms, and the launch could not slip past it.

Finance wanted ₹2.25 lakh. Sales wanted ₹1.95 lakh. Her own research pointed somewhere between. She had to choose the logic first, and the number would follow.

2. Company background

Sthaayi EV Works was founded in 2017 by Karthikeyan Valliappan, a former powertrain engineer. It sells one product family, the Saral, an electric scooter aimed at first-time EV buyers, delivery riders and small traders. In the year to March 2026 it sold 1,20,000 Saral units through 210 dealers across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. The base Saral is priced at ₹1.15 lakh and the top Saral Max at ₹1.35 lakh. Every price in this case is net of 5 per cent GST and, unless stated otherwise, ex-showroom.

The Hosur plant assembles vehicles; battery packs come together in a smaller unit at Krishnagiri; the sales and dealer-development office sits in Vellore, and a service-training centre operates in Dharmapuri. Ranipet supplies the pressed frames. Sthaayi grew while FAME, and later the PM E-DRIVE scheme, narrowed the gap between electric and petrol scooters. Its rivals for the mass buyer are TVS with the iQube, Bajaj Auto with its Chetak, Hero MotoCorp with Vida and Ola Electric. Above them sits Ather Energy, whose customers pay more for software and ride quality.

The Shikhar is Sthaayi's answer. It carries a 4.5 kWh battery, a certified range of 170 km, a seven-inch connected display, and a three-year warranty on the pack. It would be built on a dedicated line at Hosur with a capacity of 30,000 units a year. The board has approved the line. It has not approved a price.

3. The situation

Bhuvana asked the finance team for a landed cost, and Subbiah Meyyappan, the CFO, delivered it within a day. Exhibit 1 sets it out. The Shikhar costs ₹1.80 lakh to build, warrant and sell, of which the battery pack alone is ₹0.80 lakh. Subbiah's policy is a 25 per cent mark-up on landed cost, which gives ₹2.25 lakh, a number nobody can dispute because it comes from the ledger.

4. The people

Bhuvana Alagappan, Chief Product Officer, Hosur, owns the recommendation. She wants the Shikhar to make Sthaayi more than the cheap EV.

Subbiah Meyyappan, CFO, Hosur, wants every launch to clear the 25 per cent mark-up.

Sivagami Nachiappan, head of sales, Vellore, speaks for 210 dealers. Her dealers worry that a ₹2.25 lakh scooter will sit on the floor through Deepavali. She wants ₹1.95 lakh, a number a walk-in customer can compare with Ather at a glance.

Karthikeyan Valliappan, founder and CEO, Hosur, wants the launch to be remembered, and will back whichever number Bhuvana can defend.

Kim Seo-jun in Busan and Mei-Hua Tsai in Taipei watch how price affects cell and controller orders; Kalpana in Bengaluru owns the survey.

5. The options

Option A: cost-plus at ₹2.25 lakh. The price follows from Exhibit 1. It is the easiest number for finance to sign. Its cost is in Exhibit 3: at ₹2.25 lakh the survey gives 17,400 buyers and ₹78.30 crore of contribution, which is ₹12.00 crore less than option C, and it places the Shikhar ₹0.30 lakh above Ather's highest price.

Option B: competitive parity at ₹1.95 lakh. The price matches the top of the Ather band. Dealers can explain it and the line runs at capacity. Its cost is thin unit contribution of ₹0.15 lakh, or ₹45.00 crore in total, about half of option C, with no cushion if cell prices rise; it also signals a rival scooter, not a better one.

Option C: value-based at ₹2.15 lakh. The price comes from what buyers will pay for range, warranty and display, checked against cost and competitors. It yields ₹90.30 crore of contribution on 25,800 units, and leaves the line 4,200 units short of capacity. Its cost is that the number relies on a survey, that dealers will have to sell a premium of ₹0.20 lakh over Ather's top price, and that the Saral Max at ₹1.35 lakh now sits ₹0.80 lakh below.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of the three anchors, cost, competitors and customer value, tell Bhuvana, and what does each leave out?
  2. Using Exhibit 3, why does contribution peak at ₹2.15 lakh, and which price would a manager choose if she wanted to maximise units, and why would that be a mistake?
  3. How reliable is a stated-intent survey of 400 people, and what could Bhuvana do before Tuesday to test it?
  4. Which option would you recommend, and how would you respond to the CFO and the head of sales?

7. A note for the learner

The topic frames pricing as a choice between three anchors that answer different questions. Cost sets a floor: below ₹1.80 lakh, or ₹1.84 lakh if cells rise, each Shikhar loses money. Competitors set a reference: the ₹1.95 lakh top of the Ather band tells customers what they have been trained to expect. Customer value sets the ceiling: the most a buyer will pay for the benefit as she perceives it. A price that sits on only one anchor is a guess about the other two. Cost-plus dominates when there is no market evidence, competitive pricing when buyers cannot tell products apart, and value-based pricing when the product is differentiated and buyers can be asked, as with the Shikhar.

A defensible path is option C, at or near ₹2.15 lakh. The reasoning has four steps. First, Exhibit 3 shows contribution of ₹90.30 crore at ₹2.15 lakh against ₹78.30 crore for cost-plus and ₹45.00 crore for parity, so the value anchor beats both alternatives on the metric the company cares about. Second, ₹2.15 lakh clears the cost floor by ₹0.35 lakh, and by ₹0.31 lakh if the Busan increase arrives. Third, the premium over Ather is a hypothesis the launch can test, so Bhuvana should ask Sivagami to run the price in twenty dealers around Vellore and Krishnagiri for the first fortnight, with the range, warranty and app as the sales argument. Fourth, she should treat Subbiah's mark-up as a check, since ₹2.15 lakh is a 19.4 per cent mark-up on ₹1.80 lakh, and a check that passes with a margin is no reason to override the evidence.

The risk is that the survey measures stated intent, and the gap to the Saral Max needs a clear story. Bhuvana should be ready to revise in the first month.

Value-Based, Cost-Plus and Competitive Pricing

Three anchors compete for the same number. Knowing which one binds — and which one is quietly lying to you — is most of the craft.

1. Two decisions, ninety kilometres apart

On Monday, 21 September 2026, above a fabric godown in Vazirabad, Nanded, Dhanashree Sardesai opened the pricing paper she owed her board on 9 October. Taanabaana Floor Systems, where she runs product and pricing, sells a production-floor ERP to garment factories: cutting-room marker planning, line balancing, piece-rate payroll, and the compliance reports export units must produce for their buyers' audits. Sixty-one factories run on it, 742 sewing lines, at ₹4,200 per line per month — ₹3.74 crore of annual recurring revenue. The number had not moved since Sarika Mhatre, now chief financial officer, set it in 2023 by taking a 35 per cent margin on a cost to serve of ₹2,730.

Two things had unsettled it. Zunjaar Mill Cloud, the nearest rival, listed at ₹6,900 per line and still lost most head-to-head evaluations. And in June, Tarunya Apparels, a fourteen-line export shirt unit outside Nanded, renewed for a third year without asking for a discount; its production head told Shrikant Gaonkar, the implementation lead in Parbhani, that the software “paid for itself in the first month”.

Three days later, ninety kilometres north in Jalna, Ninad Kelkar faced the same question from the opposite side. Zankaar Shopfloor Devices, which he co-founded, sells a ruggedised line terminal — a touch panel and scan head bolted to the end of each sewing line — with the piece-rate payroll software that runs on it. The terminal lists at ₹23,500 against a landed cost of ₹16,006, a gross margin of 31.9 per cent that Suhas Raikar, the finance lead, defends component by component. The software bills ₹180 per operator per month; across 22 factories and 7,260 operators it yields ₹1.57 crore a year at roughly 88 per cent gross margin.

At the distributor conference on 12 October, Damini Shirodkar, who runs channel sales from Parbhani, would ask him to drop the terminal to ₹16,000 — six rupees below what it costs to land one. Suhas's cost sheet called that indefensible; Ninad was no longer certain the cost sheet was the right document to read. Both firms set a price with one anchor and are now told the anchor is wrong: Dhanashree that hers is far too low, Ninad that his is far too high.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

A pricing anchor is the class of evidence a firm treats as authoritative when deciding what to charge. Cost-plus pricing starts from the cost of producing and delivering and applies a target margin. Competitive pricing starts from what comparable sellers charge. Value-based pricing starts from the economic value created for the buyer, net of his next-best alternative, and takes a share of it.

The history explains why practitioners still talk past each other. Alfred Marshall settled the quarrel over whether cost or utility determines price by observing that both blades of the scissors cut — but firms need a rule, not a theorem, and the rule most adopted was cost-based. When R. L. Hall and C. J. Hitch surveyed British manufacturers in 1939 they found managers priced at average cost plus a conventional margin and could not describe marginal revenue at all. Competitive pricing has the older formal lineage, from Joseph Bertrand's 1883 critique of Cournot to Paul Sweezy's 1939 kinked-demand model, which explained why oligopolists watch each other's lists and move rarely. Value-based pricing is the youngest: John Forbis and Nitin Mehta gave it operational form in 1981 with “economic value to the customer”, a ladder from the incumbent's reference price to the monetised differential of the new offering, which Thomas Nagle and Reed Holden systematised from 1987. Frank Ramsey's 1927 work on optimal taxation supplies the multi-product extension: load common costs onto the least elastic offerings.

Exhibit 2. What each school will and will not sign
SchoolSignsRefuses
Cost-plusNo price is defensible unless traceable to an audited cost and a stated margin.That a cost you cannot see — a rival's, a buyer's avoided loss — should set yours.
CompetitivePrice is a position in a market; buyers evaluate in sets, so the set determines what is payable.That a value model built from your own customers is evidence, not advocacy.
Value-basedPrice should track the buyer's economics; cost is a floor and rivals a reference, but neither knows what the thing is worth.That a margin convention or a rival's list says anything about willingness to pay.

The disagreement is about evidence, not virtue: auditability, external validation, causal measurement. A practitioner who cannot say which kind her organisation will believe has not finished the analysis.

3. Mechanics: how the three numbers get built

Start with cost, which everybody thinks is simple. It is not: cost-plus has no single cost. Finance maintains two views of the same line.

Exhibit 3. Taanabaana's cost to serve, per sewing line per month, FY26

At the standing 35 per cent margin the direct view gives a floor of ₹2,925 ÷ 0.65 = ₹4,500; the loaded view gives ₹4,550 ÷ 0.65 = ₹7,000. Both are cost-plus, both honest, 56 per cent apart. The 2023 price of ₹4,200 was the direct floor of its day (₹2,730 ÷ 0.65), so Taanabaana has spent three years charging a number never intended as an answer.

The competitive anchor is easy to assemble and easy to assemble wrongly. Zunjaar lists at ₹6,900 and, at ten lines or more, settles at ₹5,500 — a realised discount of 20.3 per cent. A global apparel-ERP suite also competes, but meters named users: at a factory the size of Tarunya it quotes 56 users at ₹2,650 each, ₹1,48,400 a month, or ₹10,600 per line converted. Whoever controls the restatement controls the comparison.

The value anchor takes real work, always of one shape: find the operating variable the product moves, measure the movement, convert it to contribution. For a sewing line that is line efficiency — standard minutes produced over standard minutes available. Tarunya runs 30 operators per line on a 480-minute shift, so each line has 14,400 available minutes a day and works 26 days a month. Shrikant's study across eleven installations put efficiency at 47 per cent before line balancing and 53 per cent after.

Contribution is net of the piece rate: the cut-make-trim price is ₹135 a shirt, of which ₹55 goes to operators, ₹22 to trims, thread and packing and ₹20 to variable overhead, leaving ₹38. Across fourteen lines the factory gains ₹6,63,936 a month, ₹79.67 lakh a year. The production head's remark was arithmetic.

Here is the step most teams skip. ₹47,424 is absolute value, which is not a ceiling, because the buyer has an alternative already delivering much of it. Zunjaar's engine lifts efficiency about 3.5 points against Taanabaana's 6. The differential is 2.5 points: on 14,400 minutes that is 360 standard minutes, 20 shirts, ₹760 a line-day, ₹19,760 a line-month. Economic value to the customer is the reference price plus that differential, ₹5,500 + ₹19,760 = ₹25,260 — the price at which Tarunya is indifferent between the two products. Everything below is negotiable surplus.

Choosing inside the band is a judgement about how much of the differential the seller keeps. Dhanashree proposed ₹9,800 per line-month: that captures (₹9,800 − ₹5,500) ÷ ₹19,760 = 21.8 per cent of the differentiation value, leaves ₹15,460 unclaimed, and still returns Tarunya ₹47,424 ÷ ₹9,800 = 4.84 rupees of contribution per rupee of subscription. It sits 78.2 per cent above Zunjaar's realised price and 7.5 per cent below the global suite's line-equivalent.

4. When each anchor dominates, stated as tests

Claim one: value-based pricing requires a measurable operating variable the product demonstrably moves. Taanabaana passes — line efficiency is metered by the software itself, before and after, across eleven installations. Zankaar's terminal fails: the device does not move efficiency, the software running on it does, so the hardware is not separately value-priceable. That is the decisive asymmetry.

Claim two: competitive anchoring dominates where buyers evaluate in a set and can restate prices in a common unit cheaply. Both pass. Factory owners in Marathwada compare software quotes at trade meetings, so ₹5,500 is a live reference. Terminals are compared more readily still: a touch panel with a scan head is visibly a commodity, and Damini's distributors quote three brands on one sheet.

Claim three: cost-plus dominates where marginal cost is large relative to price and no benefit can be shown. Zankaar's hardware passes the first count — ₹16,006 landed against ₹23,500 is 68.1 per cent of revenue — and fails the second only because the software carries the benefit. Taanabaana fails both: at ₹9,800 its direct marginal cost is 29.8 per cent of price, and the benefit is already measured.

Cost-plus turns actively misleading in exactly Taanabaana's condition: low marginal cost, high value, a cost base dominated by allocations, producing a number that drifts with accounting policy rather than the market. Value-based pricing turns misleading when the model is built from adopters only — selection dressed as causation. Competitive pricing turns misleading when the rival prices on a different cost base or a different unit, which is the ₹10,600 trap.

5. Hard edges: bundles, two sides, regulation, hardware, AI

Multi-product. Only line balancing has a clean value model. Cutting-room planning saves fabric, which under a cut-make-trim contract is the buyer's, so the factory captures none of it. Ramsey's logic applies: recover common cost on the least elastic module and price the rest for attachment.

Two-sided. The compliance module's beneficiary is not its payer: a European buyer mandates the audit pack, the factory buys it, the brand captures the risk reduction. Willingness to pay collapses toward the cost of non-compliance to the factory — a distinction that cost Taanabaana a launch.

Regulated. Piece-rate payroll sits on the Minimum Wages Act, EPFO and ESIC obligations, so a module that optimises piece rates cannot claim value from suppressing earnings. Of ₹6,480 of incremental cut-make-trim revenue per line-day, ₹2,640 flows to operators and only ₹1,824 becomes factory contribution. Regulation does not forbid value pricing; it fixes who owns the value.

Hardware plus software. Zankaar's terminal has a bill of materials, a warranty provision and a channel margin, all of which make cost-plus feel inevitable. The margin stack says otherwise.

AI-native. The marker-nesting optimiser runs inference on every cutting plan, so unlike the rest of the platform its marginal cost scales with usage. That reintroduces a genuine floor per unit consumed — the one place where cost-plus reasoning has strengthened.

At the seams. Mature companies say they price on value and mostly do not. Product builds a value model, finance owns a margin floor, sales owns a discount authority, and the realised price is the outcome of the three — which is why average discount, not list, is worth auditing.

6. Nine things an expert sees that a competent practitioner misses

Cost-plus has no single cost

The tell is a floor that moves when nothing changed. Taanabaana's is ₹4,500 or ₹7,000 depending on whether product development is allocated: same convention, same month, 56 per cent apart. The obvious reading, that one is correct, is wrong: cost-plus is a family of answers indexed by an accounting choice.

A rival's price is not comparable until it is in your unit

The tell is a slide with two rupee figures and no denominator. ₹2,650 per named user and ₹9,800 per line are not the same object; the conversion to ₹10,600 assumed 56 users at fourteen lines. Assume 70 users and it becomes ₹13,250. Audit the denominator first.

Value must be differential, never absolute

The tell is a deck quoting a large value number with no named alternative. ₹47,424 a line-month is real and nearly useless as a pricing input; the relevant figure is ₹19,760, the part Zunjaar cannot deliver. Absolute value produces numbers that feel bold and collapse when a buyer says he would have got most of it anyway.

Ask who captures the gain before asking what it is worth

The tell is high measured value alongside a low attach rate. Fabric savings accrue to the brand, compliance value to the buyer, and 40.7 per cent of incremental cut-make-trim revenue to operators through the piece rate. Only the residue is priceable.

Risk reduction prices like insurance, not like output

The tell is an expected-value calculation inside the pricing model. Cutting an 18 per cent chance of a failed audit to 6 per cent on an order worth ₹1.85 crore is worth ₹22.2 lakh in expectation, and almost no owner-manager pays a tenth of that: nobody is risk-neutral about their own factory.

Realised value lags promised value; the billing does not

The tell is churn concentrated in months three to five. Line balancing needs a full style-changeover cycle before efficiency moves, and Taanabaana bills from week one. Experts delay the step-up, tie the first invoice to a measured threshold, or read early churn as a pricing artefact.

The anchor and the metric are separate decisions

The tell is a team announcing a move to value-based pricing and describing a change of unit. Taanabaana anchors on value and still meters per line, because a line is what a factory owner can count. Confusing the two yields a defensible number charged against an uncountable unit.

A price change is two decisions: the level and the path

The tell is a price card with no migration column. Moving 61 factories from ₹4,200 to ₹9,800 in one step is arithmetically identical to, and commercially very different from, moving them in two. Dhanashree steps existing customers to 80 per cent of the card — ₹7,840 and ₹4,160 — at first renewal, the rest at the second.

The three anchors triangulate; they do not vote

The tell is a paper that shows three numbers and picks the middle. Cost gives a floor below which the business dies, competitors a band outside which the buyer stops listening, value a ceiling above which the trade stops making sense. The price is a judgement about which constraint binds.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products value per user is small, heterogeneous and costly to measure, so competitive anchoring dominates and prices cluster at focal numbers. In B2B and enterprise the buyer has a profit-and-loss statement, which is what makes a value model possible; Taanabaana is a clean instance. On platforms and marketplaces the anchor differs by side: the side with measurable incremental revenue is value-priced, the side with alternatives one tap away is competitively priced. In hardware the bill of materials is visible to procurement, pushing toward cost-plus even when the margin stack argues against it. In AI products inference gives a real variable cost, so the floor binds again at the margin.

Stage matters less than is claimed, with one exception. A seed-stage company has no before-and-after data and is forced toward competitive anchoring, which it should treat as a placeholder, not a strategy. Once a firm has an instrumented installed base the value model becomes available, and a company that has not built one is under-pricing by default.

8. Three worked examples

Where value-based pricing was right

The new card is ₹9,800 per line for export units and ₹5,200 for domestic job-work units. The second comes from the same method with different inputs: job-work units run basic knits at 12 standard minutes with ₹21 of contribution, and the data shows a 4-point lift rather than 6 — 576 standard minutes, 48 pieces, ₹1,008 a line-day, ₹26,208 a line-month. At ₹5,200 that is 19.8 per cent of absolute value against 20.7 per cent for exports: similar capture, very different bases.

Where cost-plus was the wrong anchor

Zankaar's question is settled not by the bill of materials but by the margin stack over an account's life. A typical new factory takes eleven terminals and 330 operators on payroll software.

Of 38 factories offered it, 9 bought — 23.7 per cent — and two did not renew. The model was arithmetically sound and behaviourally naive: the value was a tail risk, the beneficiary the brand, the payer a cash-tight factory. Repriced at ₹78,000, a cut of 67.5 per cent, attach rose to 29 of 38, 76.3 per cent, and revenue moved from ₹21.60 lakh to ₹22.62 lakh — almost nothing gained in revenue, everything in coverage.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Cost-plus drift. Warning: the price has not changed while the product has. Diagnostic: divide today's price by today's measured value and compare with the ratio at launch. Taanabaana's capture of absolute value — ₹4,200 ÷ ₹47,424 — had fallen to 8.9 per cent, against 20.7 per cent on the new card, and three years of a ₹5,600 monthly gap across 742 lines is roughly ₹15 crore never billed.

Competitive mirroring. Warning: the pricing paper cites only rivals. Diagnostic: ask what the rival's cost base and delivered outcome are. Caught late, you have imported someone else's error as discipline.

Value theatre. Warning: a model built only from customers who adopted. Diagnostic: ask for the comparison group and the date the window opened. Caught late, it yields a price sales cannot defend, and quiet unlogged discounting.

Unit mismatch. Warning: customers asking how the bill is calculated. Diagnostic: can the production manager count the unit without opening the software? Caught late, every contract is renegotiated at once.

Path neglect. Warning: a migration plan invented after the card is signed off. Diagnostic: model churn at the actual step size, not the average. Caught late, the level was right and the business shrinks anyway.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The strongest case for value-based primacy is that it is the only anchor referencing the buyer at all, resting on the finding that firms which build value models raise realised prices without proportionate volume loss. It would be wrong if value models were systematically biased upward by adopter selection — which they demonstrably sometimes are — or if measurement cost exceeded the gain.

The strongest case for competitive primacy is behavioural: buyers do not compute economic value, they compare visible prices, and a price outside the accepted band is rejected before any value argument is heard. It would be wrong if buyers routinely ran their own payback calculations, as industrial buyers with procurement functions do.

The strongest case for cost-plus is institutional and usually caricatured. It is the only anchor with an audit trail, the only one a distributor, a tax authority or a public tender accepts without argument, and in commoditising markets it converges on the competitive answer. It would be wrong if the cost base were dominated by allocation, as Taanabaana's is, or if marginal cost were near zero, which describes most software. The AI turn has strengthened this school more than anything in thirty years.

These positions do not reconcile. They rest on different views of what a buyer is: a calculator, a comparer, or a counterparty in an institution that must justify itself.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this presents three numbers and recommends the middle one. Someone who has internalised it states which anchor binds, and why, before showing any arithmetic; builds the value model from a comparison group rather than from adopters, and says how much of the estimate is selection; treats the value figure as a ceiling approached deliberately, and can say what the unclaimed headroom buys — renewal calm, room for a second increase, a defence against the rival's response; and separates the level from the path, having seen a correct price destroy a base moved too fast.

12. What each of them decided

Dhanashree took the ₹9,800 and ₹5,200 card to her board on 9 October with the step-up path attached and the churn budget stated in advance, arguing that the binding constraint was no longer cost but credibility: at ₹9,800 Taanabaana had to be visibly better than Zunjaar, and the efficiency data said it was. Ninad cut the terminal to ₹16,000 and told the distributor conference the truth — that Zankaar now makes essentially nothing on hardware and intends to — while moving payroll software to a value-anchored price at the next renewal: a company giving away the visible thing must be exact about the invisible one.

Three questions for discussion.

  1. Taanabaana's value model rests on eleven installations that chose to adopt. What would a defensible comparison group look like across 61 factories, and what would you pay to build one?
  2. Zankaar's cut is justified by software gross profit over three years. What must be true about churn, and about who owns the operator data, for that horizon to be honest?
  3. If Taanabaana's inference cost rises fivefold, which anchor moves first — and should the price follow it?
